article_paragraphs: 2007年第十七届搞笑诺贝尔奖在卧室、餐桌与蓝天之间展开了奇妙探索。荷兰埃因霍温理工大学的约翰娜·范·布龙斯维克教授凭借对每晚与人类同床共枕的螨虫、昆虫、蜘蛛、伪蝎、甲壳类动物、细菌、藻类、蕨类和真菌进行全面细致的“床铺人口普查”而夺得生物学奖。同在床铺上做文章的还有物理学奖得主、美国哈佛大学的马哈德万与智利圣地亚哥大学的恩里克·塞尔达·维拉布兰卡，他们深入研究了床单等弹性薄片在拉力下起皱的几何与物理规律。而在阿根廷国立基尔梅斯大学，帕特里夏·阿戈斯蒂诺、圣地亚哥·普拉诺与迭戈·戈隆贝克发现抗阳痿药物伟哥（西地那非）能帮助仓鼠更快倒过时差、恢复昼夜节律，一举拿下航空学奖。

吞吐之间尽显硬核科学本色。英国放射科医生布莱恩·威特科姆与美国吞剑协会的丹·迈耶因发表极具穿透力的医学报告《吞剑及其副作用》荣膺医学奖，详尽统计了全球吞剑表演者的喉咙疼痛与食道穿孔等职业伤病。美国康奈尔大学的布莱恩·万辛克设计了通过桌下暗管自动续汤的“无底洞汤碗”，借此探测人类深不可测的食欲与视觉暗示效应，证明人在不知情下会不知不觉多喝七成热汤，从而斩获营养学奖。日本国际医疗福祉大学的山本麻由则因利用亚临界水反应从牛粪中成功提取出香草醛（即香草香精成分）而赢得化学奖，剑桥当地冰激凌名店甚至为此专门推出了纪念款香草冰淇淋。

语言、治安与军事领域的脑洞同样惊人。西班牙巴塞罗那大学的胡安·曼努埃尔·托罗、何塞普·特罗巴隆与努里娅·塞巴斯蒂安-加列斯荣获语言学奖，他们通过实验证明大鼠有时无法区分倒着说的日语和倒着说的荷兰语。澳大利亚索引专家格伦达·布朗深入剖析了英语定冠词“The”给所有试图按字母顺序排列目录的人带来的种种麻烦，幽默摘得文学奖。中国台湾的谢国桢因在2001年为一套从天花板瞬间降下的“撒网抓银行劫匪装置”申请美国专利而拿下经济学奖；美国俄亥俄州代顿市的美国空军赖特实验室则因在1994年提议研发能让敌军士兵彼此产生强烈性吸引力的化学武器“同性恋炸弹”，尴尬地捧走了和平奖。

title_en: Cow-Dung Vanilla, Bottomless Soup Bowls, and Jet-Lagged Hamsters on Viagra
subtitle_en: From Sword-Swallowing Side Effects and Bedbug Censuses to Bank-Robber Nets and the 'Gay Bomb'
article_paragraphs_en: The 17th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony in 2007 ventured from the microscopic ecosystems of our mattresses to the circadian rhythms of frequent-flying rodents. Dutch biologist Prof. Dr. Johanna E.M.H. van Bronswijk of Eindhoven University of Technology won the Biology Prize for conducting a comprehensive census of all the mites, insects, spiders, pseudoscorpions, crustaceans, bacteria, algae, ferns, and fungi with whom humans share their beds every night—an entire miniature jungle thriving in our mattress dust. Staying in the bedroom, L. Mahadevan of Harvard University and Enrique Cerda Villablanca of the University of Santiago, Chile, captured the Physics Prize for formulating the mathematical geometry and elasticity equations that govern how bedsheets and fabrics become wrinkled and draped under tension. Meanwhile, in Argentina, Patricia V. Agostino, Santiago A. Plano, and Diego A. Golombek of the National University of Quilmes won the Aviation Prize for discovering that small doses of Viagra (sildenafil) help hamsters recover up to fifty percent faster from simulated six-hour eastbound jetlag shifts.

Brave feats of ingestion and aromatic alchemy dominated the medical and food sciences. British radiologist Brian Witcombe and sword-swallower Dan Meyer earned the Medicine Prize for their penetrating British Medical Journal survey 'Sword Swallowing and Its Side Effects,' cataloging 'sword throats,' esophageal perforations, and the hazards of swallowing multiple blades at once—which Meyer memorably demonstrated live on stage at Sanders Theatre. Food psychologist Brian Wansink received the Nutrition Prize for rigging 'bottomless' bowls of tomato soup to secret under-table refill pipes, proving that visual portion cues override stomach fullness as diners unknowingly ate 73 percent more soup without feeling any fuller. And Mayu Yamamoto of the International Medical Center of Japan won the Chemistry Prize for extracting vanillin—real vanilla flavoring and fragrance—from cow dung via subcritical water reactions, inspiring Cambridge's famed Toscanini's Ice Cream shop to serve a special 'Yum-a-Moto Vanilla Twist' flavor in her honor.

Linguistic confusion, indexing headaches, and unconventional crime-and-warfare schemes completed the 2007 lineup. Juan Manuel Toro, Josep B. Trobalon, and Núria Sebastián-Gallés of the University of Barcelona took the Linguistics Prize for showing that while rats can easily distinguish spoken Japanese from spoken Dutch when played forward, the rodents are completely stumped when both languages are played backward. Australian professional indexer Glenda Browne won the Literature Prize for her definitive treatise on the definite article 'The' and the myriad headaches it inflicts on anyone trying to sort titles and entries into alphabetical order. In Taiwan, inventor Kuo Cheng Hsieh earned the Economics Prize for U.S. Patent #6,219,959, an infrared-triggered ceiling trap that catches bank robbers immediately by dropping a heavy net over them. Finally, the Peace Prize went to the U.S. Air Force Wright Laboratory in Dayton, Ohio, for a 1994 proposal to develop the so-called 'Gay Bomb'—a non-lethal aphrodisiac chemical weapon intended to make enemy soldiers become sexually irresistible to one another.

article_paragraphs: 2008年第十八届搞笑诺贝尔奖证明，哪怕没有大脑的生物或毫无药效的假药也能创造奇迹。认知科学奖颁给日本北海道大学的中垣俊之、山田裕康、小林亮、手动厚、石黑章夫与匈牙利塞格德大学的阿戈塔·托特，他们发现毫无神经系统的单细胞生物黏菌竟能解开迷宫谜题并找到最短路径。医学奖得主、杜克大学的丹·艾瑞里、麻省理工学院的丽贝卡·瓦贝尔、斯坦福大学的巴巴·希夫与欧洲工商管理学院的齐夫·卡蒙则证实，标价昂贵的假药（安慰剂）比标价低廉的假药止痛效果更好。而在意大利特伦托大学与英国牛津大学，马西米利亚诺·赞皮尼与查尔斯·斯彭斯通过电子手段修饰并调高咀嚼薯片时的咔嚓声，让吃薯片的人相信薯片比实际更酥脆新鲜，从而夺得营养学奖。

动物与植物也在各自的领地改写着规则。法国图卢兹国立兽医学校的玛丽-克里斯蒂娜·卡迪耶格、克里斯代尔·茹贝尔与米歇尔·弗朗拿下生物学奖，他们通过实测发现寄生在狗身上的跳蚤比寄生在猫身上的跳蚤跳得更高。巴西圣保罗大学的阿斯托尔福·梅洛·阿劳若与何塞·卡洛斯·马塞利诺荣获考古学奖，精确测量了一只活犰狳在考古发掘地打洞折腾时如何把历史文物地层搅得天翻地覆。瑞士联邦非人类生物技术伦理委员会与瑞士公民则因正式确立“植物拥有尊严”的法律原则，认为随意把路边野花斩首有悖道德，一举捧走和平奖。

物理、化学与社会学研究更是妙趣横生。美国斯克里普斯海洋研究所的多里安·雷默与加州大学圣迭戈分校的道格拉斯·史密斯斩获物理学奖，他们从数学上证明成堆的绳子或头发只要经过翻滚晃动，就不可避免地会自动打成死结。化学奖由两派针锋相对的学者共享：波多黎各大学的莎莉·乌皮埃尔、约瑟夫·希尔与哈佛医学院的黛博拉·安德森发现可口可乐是有效的杀精剂，而台北医学大学的洪传岳、谢仲思、吴佩与姜必宁则证明可口可乐并无杀精功效。此外，新墨西哥大学的杰弗里·米勒、乔舒亚·泰伯与布伦特·乔丹因发现职业脱衣舞娘在排卵期赚取的小费显著更高而赢得经济学奖；伦敦卡斯商学院的大卫·西姆斯则凭深情撰写的论文《你个混蛋：对组织内部愤怒体验的叙事探索》摘得文学奖。

title_en: Maze-Solving Slime Molds, Pricey Placebos, and Self-Knotting Strings
subtitle_en: From Electronically Crisped Potato Chips and Plant Dignity to the Coca-Cola Spermicide Debate
article_paragraphs_en: The 18th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony in 2008 proved that neither a brain nor real medication is strictly necessary to achieve remarkable results. The Cognitive Science Prize went to Toshiyuki Nakagaki, Hiroyasu Yamada, Ryo Kobayashi, Atsushi Tero, Akio Ishiguro, and Ágotá Tóth for demonstrating that Physarum polycephalum—a brainless, single-celled yellow slime mold—can solve a laboratory maze by withdrawing protoplasmic tubes from dead ends to connect two oat flakes along the exact shortest path. Meanwhile, Dan Ariely of Duke University, Rebecca L. Waber of MIT, Baba Shiv of Stanford University, and Ziv Carmon of INSEAD won the Medicine Prize for proving that high-priced fake medicine ($2.50 placebo pills) relieves pain significantly better than discounted low-priced fake medicine ($0.10 placebo pills). Sensory illusion also triumphed in the Nutrition Prize, awarded to Massimiliano Zampini of the University of Trento and Charles Spence of Oxford University for electronically boosting the high-frequency crunch of Pringles potato chips through headphones, tricking tasters into believing stale chips were fifteen percent crisper and fresher than they really were.

Animals and plants rewrote the rules of biology, archaeology, and constitutional ethics. Marie-Christine Cadiergues, Christel Joubert, and Michel Franc of the École Nationale Vétérinaire de Toulouse won the Biology Prize for discovering that fleas living on dogs (Ctenocephalides canis) can jump significantly higher—up to twenty-five centimeters—than fleas living on cats (Ctenocephalides felis). In Brazil, Astolfo G. Mello Araujo and José Carlos Marcelino of the University of São Paulo captured the Archaeology Prize by letting a live nine-banded armadillo burrow through an experimental test pit filled with painted potsherds, measuring just how thoroughly one armored mammal can scramble the chronological strata of human history. And in Europe, the Swiss Federal Ethics Committee on Non-Human Biotechnology (ECNH) and the citizens of Switzerland received the Peace Prize for adopting the legal principle that plants possess intrinsic moral dignity—meaning that arbitrarily decapitating roadside wildflowers without rational justification is ethically wrong.

Physics, chemistry, and workplace indignation delivered a rousing finale. Dorian Raymer of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography and Douglas Smith of the University of California, San Diego, won the Physics Prize for tumbling strings inside a rotating box thousands of times to prove mathematically that heaps of string, cords, or hair inevitably tangle themselves into complex prime knots within seconds. The Chemistry Prize brought together two rival teams on opposite sides of the same fizzy question: Sharee A. Umpierre, Joseph A. Hill, and Deborah J. Anderson won for their 1985 New England Journal of Medicine report showing that Coca-Cola (especially Diet Coke) is an effective spermicide, while Chuang-Ye Hong, C.C. Shieh, P. Wu, and B.N. Chiang of Taipei Medical University shared the prize for their 1987 study proving that it is not. Finally, Geoffrey Miller, Joshua Tybur, and Brent Jordan of the University of New Mexico won the Economics Prize for discovering that professional lap dancers earn substantially higher tips during the fertile ovulatory phase of their menstrual cycles, and David Sims of London's Cass Business School won the Literature Prize for his lovingly written organizational study, 'You Bastard: A Narrative Exploration of the Experience of Indignation within Organizations.'

article_paragraphs: 2009年第十九届搞笑诺贝尔奖在哈佛大学桑德斯剧院热闹颁出，将死磕到底的实验精神推向极致。美国加州的唐纳德·昂格尔医生独揽医学奖：为了验证母亲从小唠叨的“掰手指会得关节炎”究竟是不是真的，他坚持每天掰响左手关节至少两次、却从不碰右手，六十多年后拍片证实双手均无关节炎，在领奖台上仰天高呼“妈，你错了！”同样硬核的还有瑞士伯尔尼大学的斯特凡·博利格、斯特芬·罗斯、拉尔斯·厄斯特黑尔韦格、迈克尔·塔利与贝亚特·克诺伊比尔，五位法医通过砸击实验测定满啤酒瓶还是空啤酒瓶砸头更结实，发现空瓶因无内部气压反而更耐砸，但两者都足以敲碎人类头骨，凭此斩获和平奖。

物理、化学与生物界的发现同样令人拍案叫绝。辛辛那提大学的凯瑟琳·惠特科姆、哈佛大学的丹尼尔·利伯曼与得克萨斯大学的莉萨·夏皮罗从力学和进化角度算出女性腰椎拥有独特的楔形椎骨与前凸曲度，完美解释“为什么孕妇不会向前翻倒”，摘得物理学奖。墨西哥国立自治大学的哈维尔·莫拉莱斯、米格尔·阿帕蒂加与维克托·卡斯塔尼奥将龙舌兰酒加热气化沉积出纳米金刚石薄膜，用液体美酒造出真钻石，捧走化学奖。英国纽卡斯尔大学的凯瑟琳·道格拉斯与彼得·罗林森拿下兽医学奖，证明有名字的奶牛比无名奶牛产奶量更高；日本北里大学的田口文章、宋国富与张光磊则用大熊猫粪便中提取的耐高温细菌将厨余垃圾质量消减九成以上，夺得生物学奖。

公共服务与金融领域的黑色幽默更是入木三分。芝加哥的叶连娜·博德纳尔、拉斐尔·李与桑德拉·马里扬发明了紧急时刻可迅速拆成两个防护面罩的救生胸罩，一个留给自己、一个分给路人，荣膺公共卫生奖。爱尔兰警察局尴尬领走文学奖，因为他们向全国头号违章惯犯“Prawo Jazdy”开出了五十多张罚单，殊不知这词在波兰语里其实是“驾驶执照”。津巴布韦储备银行行长吉迪恩·戈诺因印制面额从一美分到一百万亿的钞票、帮百姓每天练习超大跨度数字而获数学奖；冰岛四大银行Kaupthing、Landsbanki、Glitnir及冰岛央行的高管与审计师则因证明小银行能瞬间变成大银行再瞬间缩水，并顺手把整个国家经济也玩成这样，拿下经济学奖。

title_en: Sixty Years of Knuckle-Cracking, Tequila Diamonds, and 100-Trillion-Dollar Bills
subtitle_en: From Emergency Gas-Mask Brassieres and Beer-Bottle Skull Physics to Named Dairy Cows
article_paragraphs_en: The 19th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony at Harvard's Sanders Theatre celebrated scientific persistence at its most personal and Bruising. California allergist Donald L. Unger claimed the Medicine Prize for a self-experiment spanning more than sixty years: determined to test his mother's stern childhood warning that cracking his fingers would ruin his joints, he diligently cracked the knuckles of his left hand at least twice a day while leaving his right hand untouched. After more than 36,500 cracks, X-rays revealed zero arthritis in either hand, prompting Unger to look skyward and declare, 'Mother, you were wrong!' Equally hard-headed was the Peace Prize team of Stephan Bolliger, Steffen Ross, Lars Oesterhelweg, Michael Thali, and Beat Kneubuehl at the University of Bern, who experimentally smashed full and empty beer bottles onto human skull models. They discovered that empty bottles are actually sturdier because internal beer pressure weakens full ones — though both easily pack enough fracture energy to crack a human cranium.

Physics, chemistry, and biology offered equally dazzling revelations. Katherine K. Whitcome of the University of Cincinnati, Daniel E. Lieberman of Harvard University, and Liza J. Shapiro of the University of Texas won the Physics Prize for analytically determining why pregnant women do not tip over forward: evolution equipped female hominins with three lumbar vertebrae wedged to increase lordosis curvature and shift the center of mass back over the hips. In Mexico, Javier Morales, Miguel Apátiga, and Victor M. Castaño of Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México captured the Chemistry Prize by vaporizing liquid tequila at high temperatures to deposit genuine crystalline diamond films. Meanwhile, Newcastle University's Catherine Douglas and Peter Rowlinson won the Veterinary Medicine Prize for proving that dairy cows given personal names produce significantly more milk than nameless cattle, while Fumiaki Taguchi, Song Guofu, and Zhang Guanglei of Japan's Kitasato University took the Biology Prize for using thermophilic bacteria extracted from giant panda feces to reduce the mass of kitchen refuse by more than 90 percent.

Public institutions and financial wizards rounded out the evening with biting satire. Elena N. Bodnar, Raphael C. Lee, and Sandra Marijan of Chicago won the Public Health Prize for inventing and patenting an emergency brassiere that detaches in seconds into two protective respiratory face masks — one for the wearer and one for a lucky bystander. Ireland's national police service, An Garda Síochána, sheepishly received the Literature Prize after issuing more than fifty traffic tickets to the country's most notorious serial traffic offender, 'Prawo Jazdy' — before realizing that 'Prawo Jazdy' is simply the Polish phrase for 'Driving License' printed at the top of every Polish permit. Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe governor Gideon Gono earned the Mathematics Prize for giving citizens daily arithmetic practice across fourteen orders of magnitude by printing banknotes ranging from one cent ($0.01) to one hundred trillion dollars ($100,000,000,000,000). Finally, the Economics Prize went to the directors, executives, and auditors of four Icelandic banks — Kaupthing Bank, Landsbanki, Glitnir Bank, and the Central Bank of Iceland — for demonstrating that tiny banks can be rapidly transformed into huge banks, and vice versa, and that the exact same trick can be performed on an entire national economy.

article_paragraphs: 2010年第二十届搞笑诺贝尔奖见证了生物智慧与草根工程学的奇妙碰撞。伦敦动物学会的卡琳娜·阿塞韦多-怀特豪斯、阿涅丝·罗莎-戈瑟兰与墨西哥的黛安娜·让德龙夺得工程学奖：她们在遥控直升机下挂载培养皿，趁鲸鱼浮出水面换气时低空掠过喷气柱，巧妙收集“鲸鱼鼻涕”来监测疾病。而在交通规划奖中，日本学者中垣俊之、手老笃史、高木清二、三枝哲、伊藤贤太郎、弓木健司、小林亮与英国的丹·贝伯、马克·弗里克继2008年让黏菌走迷宫后再度折桂：他们按东京周边城市分布摆放燕麦片，让黏菌自由觅食，长出的菌丝网络竟与现实中的东京铁路网高度吻合，堪称天然的铁路总工程师。

人体奥秘与实验室安全同样笑点密集。荷兰阿姆斯特丹大学的西蒙·里特费尔德与蒂尔堡大学的伊利亚·范比斯特发现坐过山车能显著缓解哮喘症状，摘得医学奖；英国基尔大学的理查德·斯蒂芬斯、约翰·阿特金斯与安德鲁·金斯顿通过冰水耐痛实验，证实骂脏话确实比说文明词更能缓解疼痛，捧走和平奖。新西兰奥塔哥大学的莉安·帕金、希拉·威廉姆斯与帕特里夏·普里斯特通过对照试验，证明冬日结冰路面上“把袜子套在鞋子外面穿”能大幅减少滑倒，荣膺物理学奖。美国德特里克堡的曼努埃尔·巴贝托、查尔斯·马修斯与拉里·泰勒则用实验证实微生物极易顽固附着在留胡子科学家的胡须上，拿下公共卫生奖。

动物行为、职场管理与能源金融领域的讽刺更是辛辣独到。中国学者张礼标、谭敏、朱光剑、叶剑平、洪体玉、周善义、张树义与英国布里斯托大学的加雷思·琼斯科学记录了果蝠的口交行为及其延长交配时间的作用，赢得生物学奖。意大利卡塔尼亚大学的亚历山德罗·普卢基诺、安德烈亚·拉皮萨达与切萨雷·加罗法洛用数学模型修正“彼得原理”，证明机构若随机抽签提拔员工，运作效率反而更高，斩获管理学奖。麻省理工的埃里克·亚当斯、得州农工的斯科特·索科洛夫斯基、夏威夷大学的斯蒂芬·马苏塔尼与英国石油公司因推翻“油水不相溶”的古老信念获颁化学奖；高盛、AIG、雷曼兄弟、贝尔斯登、美林与Magnetar的高管董事们则因创造出使收益最大化、风险最小化的投资新法，共同领走经济学奖。

title_en: Whale-Snot Helicopters, Slime-Mold Railways, and Random Corporate Promotions
subtitle_en: From Socks Over Shoes on Ice and Painkilling Profanity to Roller-Coaster Asthma Therapy
article_paragraphs_en: The 20th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony in 2010 showcased nature's unexpected engineers alongside grassroots mechanical ingenuity. The Engineering Prize went to Karina Acevedo-Whitehouse and Agnes Rocha-Gosselin of the Zoological Society of London and Diane Gendron of Mexico's Instituto Politécnico Nacional, who perfected a non-invasive way to collect whale snot: they strapped sterile Petri dishes to the bottom of a remote-control helicopter and flew it directly through the misty blowhole plumes of surfacing whales to monitor respiratory microbes. Meanwhile, the Transportation Planning Prize honored Japanese and British researchers Toshiyuki Nakagaki, Atsushi Tero, Seiji Takagi, Tetsu Saigusa, Kentaro Ito, Kenji Yumiki, Ryo Kobayashi, Dan Bebber, and Mark Fricker — making Nakagaki, Tero, and Kobayashi two-time laureates after their 2008 puzzle-solving slime mold prize. By arranging oat flakes to match the geography of cities around Tokyo, they let the slime mold Physarum polycephalum grow a foraging network that spontaneously mirrored the actual Tokyo rail system in efficiency and fault tolerance.

Human physiology and laboratory safety inspired equally memorable breakthroughs. Dutch researchers Simon Rietveld of the University of Amsterdam and Ilja van Beest of Tilburg University captured the Medicine Prize for discovering that riding a thrilling roller coaster can alleviate the perceived symptoms of asthma. At Keele University in the UK, Richard Stephens, John Atkins, and Andrew Kingston won the Peace Prize for plunging volunteers' hands into ice water to confirm the age-old belief that swearing aloud genuinely increases pain tolerance and relieves suffering compared with uttering neutral words. In New Zealand, Lianne Parkin, Sheila Williams, and Patricia Priest of the University of Otago conducted a randomized controlled trial on wintry Dunedin sidewalks and won the Physics Prize for proving that pedestrians slip and fall far less often on ice when they wear socks on the outside of their shoes. And the Public Health Prize reached back to a classic Fort Detrick study by Manuel Barbeito, Charles Mathews, and Larry Taylor, who sprayed bacteria onto mannequins and bearded volunteers to prove that dangerous microbes cling tenaciously to bearded scientists even after washing.

Animal behavior, corporate hierarchy, and high-stakes finance completed the 2010 roster. Libiao Zhang, Min Tan, Guangjian Zhu, Jianping Ye, Tiyu Hong, Shanyi Zhou, and Shuyi Zhang of China, together with Gareth Jones of the University of Bristol, won the Biology Prize for scientifically documenting fellatio in short-nosed fruit bats and showing that it prolongs copulation time. Italian physicists Alessandro Pluchino, Andrea Rapisarda, and Cesare Garofalo of the University of Catania claimed the Management Prize by mathematically revisiting the Peter Principle, proving via computational simulations that organizations become significantly more efficient if they promote employees completely at random. MIT's Eric Adams, Texas A&M's Scott Socolofsky, the University of Hawaii's Stephen Masutani, and British Petroleum (BP) shared the Chemistry Prize for deep-sea oil plume research that disproved the old adage that oil and water don't mix. Finally, the Economics Prize saluted the executives and directors of Goldman Sachs, AIG, Lehman Brothers, Bear Stearns, Merrill Lynch, and Magnetar for creating and promoting bold new ways to invest money that maximize financial gain and minimize financial risk for the world economy — or at least for a select portion thereof.

article_paragraphs: 2011年第二十一届搞笑诺贝尔奖将生理冲动与感官刺激研究出了花样。日本滋贺医科大学的今井真、漆畑直树、种村秀辉、田岛幸信、后藤秀昭、沟口浩一郎与村上纯一团队荣膺化学奖：为了让听障人士在火灾熟睡中也能及时逃生，他们精确测定了空气中辛辣芥末气味的理想唤醒浓度，发明出一喷就能把人呛醒的“芥末警报器”。医学奖由欧洲的米里亚姆·图克、德布拉·特兰佩、卢克·瓦洛普与美澳的马修·刘易斯、彼得·斯奈德、罗伯特·费尔德曼、罗伯特·皮耶扎克、大卫·达比、保罗·马鲁夫团队共享，他们证实当人类强烈憋尿时，克制冲动的长远决策会变得更英明，但需要快速注意力的认知决策则会变得更糟糕。

动物、运动与人类心理同样妙趣横生。英奥荷匈学者安娜·威尔金森、娜塔莉·塞班茨、伊莎贝拉·曼德尔与路德维希·胡贝尔耗时训练红腿陆龟打哈欠，最终凭《没有证据表明红腿陆龟存在传染性打哈欠》摘得生理学奖。达里尔·格温与大卫·伦茨则因发现澳洲雄性吉丁虫把棕色凹凸纹路的澳洲啤酒瓶误当成性感雌虫、顶着烈日拼命与之交配而夺得生物学奖。法国与荷兰学者菲利普·佩兰、西里尔·佩罗、多米尼克·德维泰尔纳、布鲁诺·拉加吕和赫尔曼·金马查明了为什么铁饼运动员旋转投掷后会头晕而链球运动员却不会，捧走物理学奖；挪威奥斯陆大学的卡尔·哈尔沃·泰根因探究人们日常为何叹气获心理学奖；斯坦福大学的约翰·佩里则凭“结构化拖延理论”——想当高效人士就要靠做重要事情来逃避更重要的事情——斩获文学奖。

街头治理与神学算术更是贡献了年度名场面。立陶宛维尔纽斯市市长阿图拉斯·佐卡斯亲自驾驶装甲运兵车直接碾过违章停放的奔驰豪车，霸气捧走和平奖。多伦多大学的约翰·森德斯获公共安全奖，他在高速公路实验中让遮阳面罩反复落下遮住司机双眼以测试盲开极限。数学奖则颁给先后预言世界末日降临却屡屡落空的多萝西·马丁、帕特·罗伯逊、伊丽莎白·克莱尔·先知、李长林、克雷多尼亚·姆韦林德与哈罗德·坎平六位预言家，感谢他们用一次次算错的末日预言谆谆告诫世人：做数学假设和计算时千万要格外谨慎！

title_en: Wasabi Fire Alarms, Full-Bladder Decision-Making, and Tank-Crushed Luxury Cars
subtitle_en: From Beer-Bottle-Loving Beetles and Structured Procrastination to Failed Doomsday Prophets
article_paragraphs_en: The 21st First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony in 2011 explored urgent bodily impulses and sensory wake-up calls. Japanese researchers Makoto Imai, Naoki Urushihata, Hideki Tanemura, Yukinobu Tajima, Hideaki Goto, Koichiro Mizoguchi, and Junichi Murakami won the Chemistry Prize for determining the ideal airborne density of pungent horseradish (wasabi) needed to rouse sleeping people during a fire emergency, and applying that knowledge to invent the Wasabi Alarm — a lifesaver for deaf and hard-of-hearing sleepers whose trigeminal nerves react instantly to allyl isothiocyanate mist. Meanwhile, the Medicine Prize was shared by two international teams — Mirjam Tuk, Debra Trampe, and Luk Warlop of Europe, and Matthew Lewis, Peter Snyder, Robert Feldman, Robert Pietrzak, David Darby, and Paul Maruff of the USA and Australia — for demonstrating that when people have an acute urge to urinate, 'inhibitory spillover' helps them make better impulse-control decisions on some tasks, while making significantly worse decisions on others.

Animal habits, athletic dizziness, and everyday human quirks filled the middle of the program. Anna Wilkinson, Natalie Sebanz, Isabella Mandl, and Ludwig Huber earned the Physiology Prize for spending months training a red-footed tortoise named Alexandra to yawn on cue, ultimately publishing 'No Evidence of Contagious Yawning in the Red-Footed Tortoise.' Entomologists Darryl Gwynne and David Rentz won the Biology Prize for discovering that male Australian jewel beetles tragically mistake discarded brown 'stubby' beer bottles — whose dimpled glass mimics giant female wing covers — for mates, refusing to leave the bottles even as they bake in the sun. In sports science, Philippe Perrin, Cyril Perrot, Dominique Deviterne, Bruno Ragaru, and Herman Kingma won the Physics Prize for determining why discus throwers become dizzy while spinning whereas hammer throwers do not. University of Oslo psychologist Karl Halvor Teigen claimed the Psychology Prize for investigating why people sigh in everyday life, and Stanford philosopher John Perry took the Literature Prize for his Theory of Structured Procrastination: to be a high achiever, always work on something important as a way to avoid doing something even more important.

Municipal enforcement, highway daring, and apocalyptic arithmetic provided an unforgettable finale. Arturas Zuokas, the mayor of Vilnius, Lithuania, rolled away with the Peace Prize for personally demonstrating that the problem of illegally parked luxury cars blocking bike lanes can be solved by running them over with an armored BTR tank. University of Toronto professor John Senders received the Public Safety Prize for his classic 1967 highway experiments in which he drove an automobile down a major road while a mechanical visor repeatedly flapped down over his eyes to measure driver attentional demand. And the Mathematics Prize honored six doomsday predictors — Dorothy Martin (who predicted the world would end in 1954), Pat Robertson (1982), Elizabeth Clare Prophet (1990), Lee Jang Rim (1992), Credonia Mwerinde (1999), and Harold Camping (September 6, 1994 and October 21, 2011) — for teaching the world to be extra careful when making mathematical assumptions and calculations.

article_paragraphs: 2012年第二十二届搞笑诺贝尔奖给盲目迷信精密仪器与套娃式公文的现代社会敲响了幽默警钟。美国学者克雷格·贝内特、阿比盖尔·贝尔德、迈克尔·米勒与乔治·沃尔福德夺得神经科学奖：他们把一条死大西洋鲑鱼推进核磁共振仪，给死鱼看人类悲喜照片并做常规统计，证明只要忽略多重比较校正，复杂仪器连死鱼脑子里都能扫出“善解人意的脑部活动信号”。日本学者栗原一贵与冢田浩二发明了专治话痨的“话语干扰器”，让说话者以微秒级延迟听到自己的声音，触发听觉延迟反馈干扰令其瞬间舌头打结，摘得声学奖。美国政府问责署更因发布一份《关于报告的报告的报告》，并在文中郑重建议再准备一份《关于这份关于报告的报告的报告的报告》，捧走文学奖。

日常物理与化学谜题同样被拆解得明明白白。美英学者约瑟夫·凯勒、雷蒙德·戈德斯坦、帕特里克·沃伦与罗宾·鲍尔推导出决定人类马尾辫形状与摆动规律的统计物理平衡方程，荣膺物理学奖（组委会现场还特意为凯勒补发了1999年漏署名的茶壶嘴不滴水物理学奖，使其成为双料得主）。加州大学的鲁斯兰·克雷切特尼科夫与汉斯·迈耶因研究人端着咖啡杯走路时步伐频率如何激发液体晃动共振而导致咖啡洒出，拿下流体力学奖。瑞典与卢旺达学者约翰·彼得松则解开了瑞典安德斯勒夫镇部分新房居民洗澡后金发莫名变绿的谜团——源于热水在全新铜管中浸泡过夜溶出的铜离子，凭此获颁化学奖。

生物、心理、医学与军工转型的跨界研究更是脑洞大开。荷兰与秘鲁、俄罗斯学者阿妮塔·埃尔兰、罗尔夫·兹万与图利奥·瓜达卢佩发现《身体向左倾斜会让埃菲尔铁塔看起来更小》，斩获心理学奖（颁奖两天后前两位作者还在荷兰喜结连理）。著名灵长类学家弗朗斯·德瓦尔与珍妮弗·波科尼证实黑猩猩仅凭观看同伴臀部的照片就能准确认出对方是谁，拿下解剖学奖。法国医生埃马纽埃尔·本-苏桑与米歇尔·安东涅蒂获医学奖，他们严肃指导同行在做结肠镜检查时如何排空肠道可燃气体、把“患者在检查中发生体内爆炸”的概率降到最低；俄罗斯SKN公司则因把老旧苏联弹药转化为全新纳米钻石，名副其实地捧走和平奖。

title_en: Dead Salmon Brain Scans, the SpeechJammer Gun, and Coffee-Sloshing Dynamics
subtitle_en: From Ponytail Physics and Chimpanzee Rear-End Recognition to Non-Exploding Colonoscopies
article_paragraphs_en: The 22nd First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony in 2012 delivered a masterclass in statistical humility and bureaucratic recursion. American neuroscientists Craig Bennett, Abigail Baird, Michael Miller, and George Wolford won the Neuroscience Prize for placing a dead Atlantic salmon into an fMRI scanner, showing the dead fish photographs of humans in social situations, and demonstrating that without proper multiple-comparisons correction, complex brain-imaging instruments and simple statistics will happily detect 'meaningful brain activity' in a deceased fish. Japanese researchers Kazutaka Kurihara and Koji Tsukada captured the Acoustics Prize for inventing the SpeechJammer — a directional microphone-and-speaker device that disrupts a person's speech by playing back their own spoken words with a fraction-of-a-second delay. And the US Government General Accountability Office (GAO) won the Literature Prize for issuing a report about reports about reports that officially recommends the preparation of a report about the report about reports about reports.

Everyday physics and domestic mysteries received equally rigorous mathematical treatment. Joseph Keller of the USA and Raymond Goldstein, Patrick Warren, and Robin Ball of the UK shared the Physics Prize for calculating the balance of forces and statistical physics equations that shape and move the hair in a human ponytail (in a special ceremony announcement, organizers also corrected a 1999 oversight by awarding Keller a belated share of the 1999 Physics Prize for calculating how to make a teapot spout that does not drip). Fluid Dynamics Prize laureates Rouslan Krechetnikov and Hans Mayer of UC Santa Barbara analyzed the dynamics of liquid sloshing to explain why people walking with a cup of coffee almost inevitably spill it right around their seventh step. Meanwhile, environmental engineer Johan Pettersson of Sweden and Rwanda won the Chemistry Prize for solving the puzzle of why residents in certain newly built houses in Anderslöv, Sweden, found their blonde hair turning green — tracing the culprit to hot water sitting overnight in uncoated new copper pipes.

Psychology, primatology, clinical safety, and disarmament rounded out the night. Dutch and Peruvian researchers Anita Eerland, Rolf Zwaan, and Tulio Guadalupe won the Psychology Prize for their study 'Leaning to the Left Makes the Eiffel Tower Seem Smaller,' showing that subtle body posture biases numerical magnitude estimates (Eerland and Zwaan celebrated by getting married in the Netherlands two days after the ceremony). Primatologists Frans de Waal and Jennifer Pokorny received the Anatomy Prize for discovering that chimpanzees can identify other individual chimpanzees and match their faces simply by looking at photographs of their rear ends. French physicians Emmanuel Ben-Soussan and Michel Antonietti earned the Medicine Prize for advising doctors who perform therapeutic colonoscopies on how to prevent their patients' intestines from exploding during electrocautery. Finally, Russia's SKN Company, represented by Igor Petrov, took home the Peace Prize for converting old Russian military ammunition into shiny new nanodiamonds.

article_paragraphs: 2013年第二十三届搞笑诺贝尔奖证明，哪怕脚下推着粪球，心中也能装着浩瀚宇宙。瑞典、澳洲、南非等地学者玛丽·达克、艾米莉·贝尔德、马库斯·伯恩、克拉克·朔尔茨与埃里克·瓦兰特斩获生物学与天文学联合奖：他们给屎壳郎戴上小纸帽并在天象馆实验，首次证实迷路的屎壳郎竟能靠仰望银河系的光带导航回家！物理学奖得主阿尔贝托·米内蒂、尤里·伊万年科、杰尔马娜·卡佩利尼、娜迪亚·多米尼奇与弗朗切斯科·拉夸尼蒂则通过悬吊减重模拟发现，若把人类和池塘搬到月球等低重力环境，人真能施展“水上漂”跑过池塘水面。

医学、化学与考古学家的奉献精神同样令人肃然起敬。日本与中国学者内山雅照、金相元、张祺、平井敏仁、天野笃、判田久与新见正则给做完心脏移植手术的小鼠播放歌剧《茶花女》，发现听歌剧的小鼠免疫排斥更少、术后存活期显著延长，荣膺医学奖。今井真介、柘植信昭、友竹宗昭、长留吉朗、泽田、长田敏行与熊谷英彦因发现催泪因子合成酶、证明洋葱让人流泪的生化过程比原先以为的复杂得多而摘得化学奖。考古学家布赖恩·克兰德尔和彼得·斯塔尔更是狠人中的狠人：为查明人类消化道会溶解哪些小型哺乳动物骨骼，他们把死鼩鼱稍微水煮后不经咀嚼整只生吞下肚，连续数日仔细筛查排泄物，硬核捧走考古学奖。

心理、概率与社会奇闻同样精彩绝伦。洛朗·贝格、布拉德·布什曼、乌尔曼·泽尔胡尼、巴蒂斯特·苏布拉与迈赫迪·乌拉巴通过安慰剂实验证实“自以为喝醉的人也会觉得自己很有魅力”，拿下心理学奖。伯特·托尔坎普、玛丽·哈斯凯尔、弗里莎·兰福德、大卫·罗伯茨与科林·摩根斩获概率学奖，发现奶牛趴着越久越可能很快站起来，但一旦站起来就很难预测它何时再趴下。已故美国发明家古斯塔诺·皮佐因设计用活板门把劫机犯掉入舱底打包封装、再从弹舱门挂降落伞空投给地面警察的防劫机系统获安全工程奖；泰国医生卡西安·班加纳达等七人因发表《暹罗阴茎切除流行病的外科处理》、推荐实施再植术——“除非被鸭子吃掉了一部分”而获公共卫生奖；白俄罗斯总统卢卡申科因立法禁止公共场合鼓掌，与因“鼓掌罪”逮捕独臂男子的白俄罗斯国家警察共同领走和平奖。

title_en: Milky Way Dung Beetles, Pond-Running on the Moon, and Swallowing a Boiled Shrew
subtitle_en: From Opera-Loving Heart-Transplant Mice and Parachuting Hijackers to Duck-Eaten Amputations
article_paragraphs_en: The 23rd First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony in 2013 proved that even creatures rolling balls of manure can look to the stars. Marie Dacke, Emily Baird, Marcus Byrne, Clarke Scholtz, and Eric J. Warrant won the Joint Prize in Biology and Astronomy for fitting nocturnal dung beetles with tiny cardboard caps and testing them under the dome of the Johannesburg Planetarium, discovering that lost dung beetles orient themselves and roll straight home by gazing up at the Milky Way. Equally cosmic was the Physics Prize, awarded to Alberto Minetti, Yuri Ivanenko, Germana Cappellini, Nadia Dominici, and Francesco Lacquaniti for strapping harnessed volunteers over a wading pool to prove that humans would be physically capable of running across the surface of a pond — provided those people and that pond were in the low gravity of the Moon.

Medical, chemical, and archaeological dedication reached heroic extremes. Masateru Uchiyama, Xiangyuan Jin, Qi Zhang, Toshihito Hirai, Atsushi Amano, Hisashi Bashuda, and Masanori Niimi won the Medicine Prize for playing Verdi's opera La Traviata to mice that had just received heart transplants, demonstrating that opera-listening mice enjoyed stronger immune regulation and survived significantly longer than mice exposed to single-frequency tones. Shinsuke Imai, Nobuaki Tsuge, Muneaki Tomotake, Yoshiaki Nagatome, H. Sawada, Toshiyuki Nagata, and Hidehiko Kumagai earned the Chemistry Prize for discovering 'lachrymatory factor synthase,' proving that the biochemical process by which onions make people cry is far more complicated than scientists had realized. And archaeologists Brian Crandall and Peter Stahl claimed the Archaeology Prize for parboiling a dead shrew, swallowing it whole without chewing, and painstakingly sifting through everything excreted over subsequent days to see which micro-mammalian bones dissolve inside the human digestive tract.

Psychology, bovine probability, and surreal public policy completed the night. Laurent Bègue, Brad Bushman, Oulmann Zerhouni, Baptiste Subra, and Medhi Ourabah won the Psychology Prize for confirming by experiment that people who merely think they are drunk also think they are remarkably attractive ('beauty is in the eye of the beer holder'). Bert Tolkamp, Marie Haskell, Fritha Langford, David Roberts, and Colin Morgan captured the Probability Prize for two related dairy discoveries: first, the longer a cow has been lying down, the more likely that cow will soon stand up; and second, once a cow stands up, you cannot easily predict how soon it will lie down again. The Safety Engineering Prize honored the late Gustano Pizzo for his 1972 patent on an anti-hijacking system that drops an airplane hijacker through trap doors, seals him into a capsule, and parachutes him through bomb bay doors to waiting police on the ground. Thailand's Kasian Bhanganada, Tu Chayavatana, Chumporn Pongnumkul, Anunt Tonmukayakul, Piyasakol Sakolsatayadorn, Krit Komaratal, and Henry Wilde won the Public Health Prize for their report 'Surgical Management of an Epidemic of Penile Amputations in Siam' — techniques they recommend except in cases where the amputated penis had been partially eaten by a duck. Finally, the Peace Prize went jointly to Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, for making it illegal to applaud in public, and to the Belarus State Police, for arresting a one-armed man for applauding.

article_paragraphs: 2014年第二十四届搞笑诺贝尔奖用严谨数据解答了喜剧片里的百年老梗。日本北里大学的马渕清资、田中健诚、内岛大地与酒井利奈夺得物理学奖：他们用鞋底踩踏测力板上的香蕉皮，测出香蕉皮内侧多糖滤泡凝胶微囊在重压下会破裂化作润滑液膜，使摩擦系数骤降至0.07，比普通地板滑六倍。中国与加拿大学者刘建刚、李军、冯路、李凌、田捷与李康则聚焦“面部空想性错视”，通过脑成像揭示那些在烤吐司面包上看到耶稣面孔的人，大脑面孔区究竟发生了怎样的神经活动，荣膺神经科学奖。

动物磁场、暗黑人格与艺术止痛同样令人大开眼界。捷克、德国与赞比亚的弗拉斯蒂米尔·哈特、佩特拉·诺瓦科娃、海内克·布尔达等十二位学者耗时两年记录70只狗的数千次排泄，证实狗狗在排便和排尿时喜欢将身体轴线与地球南北地磁线对齐，摘得生物学奖。雅罗斯拉夫·弗莱格、扬·哈夫利切克、伊特卡·哈努绍娃-林多娃与大卫·哈瑙尔、纳伦·拉马克里希南、莉萨·赛弗里德因调查养猫（弓形虫感染与猫咬伤）是否会危及人类精神健康而共享公共卫生奖。彼得·乔纳森、艾米·琼斯与明娜·莱昂斯发现习惯熬夜的人比早起者平均更自恋、更具操纵欲且心理变态倾向更高，捧走心理学奖；意大利学者玛丽娜·德托马索、米歇尔·萨尔达罗与保罗·利夫雷亚用强激光束照射受试者手部，证实欣赏优美名画比看丑陋画作更能减轻疼痛，拿下艺术奖。

极地探险、急救偏方与国民经济核算更是妙趣横生。挪威学者艾吉尔·雷默斯与辛德雷·埃夫特斯托尔假扮成北极熊去悄悄接近斯瓦尔巴群岛的驯鹿，测试驯鹿的逃跑反应，夺得北极科学奖。美印医生伊恩·汉弗莱斯、索娜尔·萨赖亚、沃尔特·贝伦基与詹姆斯·德沃金因用腌猪肉条塞进患儿鼻腔、成功止住罕见病引发的致命鼻出血而获医学奖。西班牙学者拉奎尔·鲁维奥、安娜·霍夫雷、贝伦·马丁、特雷莎·艾梅里奇与玛格丽塔·加里加从婴儿粪便中分离出乳酸菌作为益生菌发酵剂来制作发酵香肠，斩获营养学奖；意大利国家统计局（ISTAT）则因率先响应欧盟指令，自豪地将卖淫、毒品交易与走私收入纳入官方国民经济统计规模，领走经济学奖。

title_en: Banana-Peel Tribology, Jesus in Toast, and Geomagnetic Pooping Dogs
subtitle_en: From Cured-Pork Nosebleed Packing and Polar-Bear Disguises to Infant-Feces Probiotic Sausages
article_paragraphs_en: The 24th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony in 2014 brought hard numbers to slapstick comedy and pareidolia. Japanese researchers Kiyoshi Mabuchi, Kensei Tanaka, Daichi Uchijima, and Rina Sakai of Kitasato University won the Physics Prize for measuring the exact frictional coefficient between a shoe, a banana skin, and a linoleum floor when a person steps on a banana peel — showing that squished polysaccharide follicular gel globules slash friction down to 0.07, making banana peels six times slipperier than bare floors. Meanwhile, Jiangang Liu, Jun Li, Lu Feng, Ling Li, Jie Tian, and Kang Lee of China and Canada captured the Neuroscience Prize for their fMRI study 'Seeing Jesus in Toast,' mapping the neural activity in the brain's fusiform face area when people perceive illusory faces in random noise or burnt breakfast bread.

Magnetic canines, nocturnal personalities, and laser-zapped art lovers took center stage next. A twelve-member team from the Czech Republic, Germany, and Zambia — Vlastimil Hart, Petra Nováková, Erich Pascal Malkemper, Sabine Begall, Vladimír Hanzal, Miloš Ježek, Tomáš Kušta, Veronika Němcová, Jana Adámková, Kateřina Benediktová, Jaroslav Červený, and Hynek Burda — won the Biology Prize for documenting thousands of canine bathroom breaks over two years to prove that when dogs defecate and urinate under calm geomagnetic conditions, they prefer to align their bodies with Earth's north-south magnetic field lines. The Public Health Prize was shared by Jaroslav Flegr, Jan Havlíček, and Jitka Hanušova-Lindova, along with David Hanauer, Naren Ramakrishnan, and Lisa Seyfried, for investigating whether owning a cat is mentally hazardous to humans due to latent Toxoplasma gondii infection and cat-bite-linked depression. Psychologists Peter K. Jonason, Amy Jones, and Minna Lyons won the Psychology Prize for amassing evidence that night owls who habitually stay up late are, on average, more narcissistic, more manipulative, and more psychopathic ('Dark Triad' traits) than early risers. And Italian researchers Marina de Tommaso, Michele Sardaro, and Paolo Livrea won the Art Prize for shooting volunteers in the hand with a powerful laser beam to prove people suffer less pain while gazing at a beautiful painting by Botticelli than while staring at an ugly painting.

Arctic masquerades, savory emergency medicine, and creative national accounting closed the show. Norwegian researchers Eigil Reimers and Sindre Eftestøl won the Arctic Science Prize for dressing up in white polar-bear disguises on the island of Edgeøya to test how Svalbard reindeer react when approached by humans disguised as polar bears. Ian Humphreys, Sonal Saraiya, Walter Belenky, and James Dworkin of the USA and India received the Medicine Prize for successfully treating 'uncontrollable' life-threatening nosebleeds in a patient with Glanzmann thrombasthenia by packing the nasal cavity with strips of cured salted pork. Spanish food scientists Raquel Rubio, Anna Jofré, Belén Martín, Teresa Aymerich, and Margarita Garriga earned the Nutrition Prize for isolating lactic acid bacteria from infant feces to use as probiotic starter cultures for tasty fermented sausages. Finally, ISTAT — the Italian government's National Institute of Statistics — proudly claimed the Economics Prize for taking the lead in fulfilling a European Union mandate to boost the official size of its national economy by including revenues from prostitution, illegal drug sales, smuggling, and other unlawful financial transactions between willing participants.

article_paragraphs: 2015年第25届搞笑诺贝尔奖在哈佛大学桑德斯剧院迎来银禧盛典，科学家们率先对生物演化与流体物理发起奇袭。智利学者布鲁诺·格罗西团队斩获生物学奖：他们把一根配重木棍绑在活鸡屁股后面改变身体重心，小鸡走路的姿态便瞬间从膝盖弯曲变成髋部驱动，完美复刻出远古霸王龙的威猛步伐。美籍华裔学者胡立德与杨佩良团队则凭动物园排尿录像摘得物理学奖，证实几乎所有体重超过三公斤的哺乳动物，无论猫狗、山羊还是大象，排空膀胱的时间都恒定在二十一秒左右。化学奖颁给了美澳学者奥蒙德、拉斯顿与韦斯等人，他们利用尿素与高速涡流流体装置解开缠结的蛋白质，硬生生把煮熟的鸡蛋“部分变回”生鸡蛋。

在痛觉与医学考场上，研究者们展现了惊人的献身精神。生理学与昆虫学奖由美国学者贾斯汀·施密特与迈克尔·史密斯共享：前者尝遍天下毒虫创立“施密特蛰痛指数”；后者亲自抓蜜蜂在自己全身二十五个部位反复蛰刺，用血泪绘出人体疼痛地图——头皮、中趾尖与上臂最轻，而鼻孔、上唇和阴茎干最痛彻心扉。英国与加拿大等国的阿什当、卡里姆团队获诊断医学奖，证实只需开车载患者经过减速带，凭剧痛反应就能准确诊断急性阑尾炎。医学奖则由日本学者木俣肇与斯洛伐克的塞莱茨、杜尔佳科娃团队共享，前者证实激烈接吻能显著缓解皮肤过敏反应，后者则测出热吻后女性唾液中竟能长久检出男性的遗传物质。

数学与人文社科奖项同样妙趣横生。奥地利学者奥伯扎彻与格拉默获数学奖，通过计算机数学模拟证实摩洛哥历史上的“嗜血苏丹”穆莱·伊斯梅尔在三十年间生育八百八十八个孩子并非神话，每天只需行房约一次即可达成。荷兰丁格曼斯、托雷拉与恩菲尔德凭文学奖发现，“啊（啥）？”这个疑问词几乎存在于人类每一种语言中，尽管他们也不太确定原因。管理学奖得主伯尼尔等人发现，童年历经地震、海啸或火山爆发却毫发无损的企业总裁，成年后在商界更酷爱冒险博弈。最绝的是经济学奖得主泰国曼谷大都会警察局：若警员当场拒绝收受贿赂，警局就直接发给他们额外现金奖金，用魔法打败魔法。

title_en: 2015: The 21-Second Law of Urination, Plunger-Tailed Dino-Chickens & Un-Boiled Eggs
subtitle_en: The 25th Silver Jubilee Ceremony: From Whole-Body Bee-Sting Maps to a Bloodthirsty Sultan's Mathematical Harem
article_paragraphs_en: The 25th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony celebrated its silver jubilee at Harvard's Sanders Theatre by turning evolutionary biology and fluid dynamics upside down. Chilean biologist Bruno Grossi and his colleagues captured the Biology Prize by strapping a weighted wooden stick—resembling a miniature toilet plunger—onto the rear ends of growing chickens. The added counterweight shifted the birds' center of mass backward, forcing their femurs into a more horizontal posture and switching their locomotion from knee-driven to hip-driven strides, uncannily recreating the walk of extinct non-avian theropod dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus rex. Meanwhile, Patricia Yang, David Hu, Jonathan Pham, and Jerome Choo claimed the Physics Prize after filming animals relieving themselves at Zoo Atlanta. Their fluid-dynamics equations proved the 'Law of Urination': nearly all mammals weighing over three kilograms—whether cats, goats, or elephants—empty their bladders in roughly 21 seconds (plus or minus 13 seconds), thanks to longer urethras amplifying gravitational flow in larger beasts.

In the realms of chemistry and extreme human endurance, researchers displayed breathtaking ingenuity and personal sacrifice. Australian and American chemists led by Callum Ormonde, Colin Raston, and Gregory Weiss won the Chemistry Prize for inventing a chemical recipe to partially un-boil a hard-boiled egg, using urea and a high-shear vortex fluidic device to untangle and refold coagulated lysozyme proteins. The Physiology and Entomology Prize went jointly to two legends of self-inflicted agony: Justin Schmidt, who painstakingly cataloged insect venom agony in his poetic 'Schmidt Sting Pain Index,' and Cornell researcher Michael L. Smith, who held live honeybees by the wings and pressed them against 25 locations on his own body three times each. Smith's anatomical pain map revealed that the skull, middle toe tip, and upper arm barely hurt, whereas the nostril, upper lip, and penis shaft deliver electrifying torment.

Medical diagnostics and human intimacy yielded equally unforgettable insights. A British-led team including Helen Ashdown, Diallah Karim, and Anthony Harnden won the Diagnostic Medicine Prize for demonstrating that acute appendicitis can be diagnosed with 97 percent sensitivity simply by asking patients whether they felt excruciating pain when driven over speed bumps on their way to the hospital. The Medicine Prize was shared by Japan's Hajime Kimata—who proved that 30 minutes of intense kissing (or sexual intercourse) significantly reduces allergic skin wheal responses and allergen-specific IgE production—and Slovakian researchers led by Jaroslava Durdiaková and Peter Celec, who quantified how long male DNA persists in female saliva after passionate French kissing. Over in Mathematics, Austria's Elisabeth Oberzaucher and Karl Grammer used computer simulations to verify whether Morocco's Sharifian Emperor Moulay Ismael the Bloodthirsty really fathered 888 children between 1697 and 1727, concluding that he needed a harem of only 65 to 110 women and roughly one copulation per day.

Finally, language, risk-taking, and anti-corruption took center stage in the social sciences. Linguists Mark Dingemanse, Francisco Torreira, and Nick Enfield earned the Literature Prize for discovering that the syllable 'Huh?'—or a nearly identical questioning grunt—exists in every human language they sampled across the globe, and for candidly admitting they were not completely sure why. Management Prize winners Gennaro Bernile, Vineet Bhagwat, and P. Raghavendra Rau showed that corporate CEOs who survived childhood natural disasters such as earthquakes, tsunamis, or wildfires without dire personal loss grew up with a lifelong fondness for risky financial gambles. Topping off the evening, the Economics Prize went to the Bangkok Metropolitan Police in Thailand, who tackled traffic corruption by offering officers a 10,000-baht cash bonus every time they refused to accept a bribe.

article_paragraphs: 2016年第26届搞笑诺贝尔奖向人类中心主义发起了最荒诞的挑战。英国两位奇人共同摘得生物学奖：牛津学者查尔斯·福斯特为了体察万物，先后在荒野中像獾一样钻进地洞生吞蚯蚓、像水獭捕鱼、像鹿和狐狸一样流浪；设计师托马斯·思韦茨则厌倦了做人的焦虑，专门定制四足行走的假肢与人工瘤胃，装扮成山羊混进阿尔卑斯山羊群同吃同住了三天。同样沉迷自然的瑞典作家弗雷德里克·舍贝里则凭三卷本自传摘得文学奖，深情记述了自己在孤岛上收集死苍蝇与活食蚜蝇的隐秘快乐。

物理与生殖科学的碰撞擦出了意想不到的静电火花。已故埃及学者艾哈迈德·沙菲克荣膺生殖学奖，他耗时多年给大鼠和人类男性穿上涤纶、纯棉与羊毛材质的小裤衩，发现纯涤纶内裤产生的静电势场会导致公鼠性欲骤降、男性精子锐减。匈牙利与瑞典的霍瓦特、奥克松团队荣获物理学奖，揭开了偏振光的生态谜团：白马最不招马蝇叮咬是因为白毛反射非偏振光；而公墓里抛光的黑色墓碑反射出酷似水面的水平偏振光，竟成了诱骗蜻蜓疯狂产卵的致命陷阱。

在感官与大脑的迷宫里，人类的直觉被轻易戏耍。德国吕贝克大学的赫尔姆兴与施普伦格团队斩获医学奖，证实如果身体左侧奇痒难耐，只需对着镜子抓挠身体右侧，就能靠视觉镜像欺骗大脑而瞬间止痒。日本学者东山笃规与足立浩平获知觉奖，他们系统验证了日本传统“股立窥景”效应，证明当人弯下腰从两腿之间倒着往后看世界时，远处景物在视觉上会显得更小更近。心理学奖得主德贝与弗舒尔团队则找来一千名骗子询问撒谎频率，并严肃评估该不该相信骗子给出的答案。

最后三项大奖对现代社会的浮夸祭出了辛辣手术刀。加拿大滑铁卢大学的佩尼库克团队凭论文《论对伪深刻狗屁言论的接收与识别》荣获和平奖，证明容易被空洞玄学词汇拼凑的心灵鸡汤感动的人普遍缺乏分析思维。新西兰阿维斯团队获经济学奖，他们让消费者给几块普通岩石评估“品牌人格”，人们竟纷纷夸石头“自信迷人”或“诚实可靠”，一举戳穿营销学泡沫。化学奖则颁给了德国大众汽车公司，讽刺其发明只在尾气检测时才自动开启减排模式的作弊软件。

title_en: 2016: The Prosthetic GoatMan of the Alps, Polyester Underpants for Rats & The Brand Personality of Rocks
subtitle_en: The 26th Ceremony: When Oxford Philosophers Eat Earthworms in Badger Burrows and Psychologists Ask a Thousand Liars About Honesty
article_paragraphs_en: The 26th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony launched a frontal assault on human exceptionalism by honoring researchers who literally stepped into the skins—or hooves—of other species. The Biology Prize went jointly to two British adventurers: Oxford polymath Charles Foster, who spent months living in the wild as a badger (sleeping in a hillside burrow and munching earthworms), an urban fox, an otter, a red deer, and a swift; and designer Thomas Thwaites, who built custom prosthetic forelimbs, hindlimbs, and an artificial rumen so he could spend three days grazing on all fours among a herd of Alpine goats to 'take a holiday from being human.' A kindred spirit in the natural world, Swedish entomologist Fredrik Sjöberg, won the Literature Prize for his three-volume autobiographical masterpiece celebrating the quiet, obsessive bliss of collecting dead flies—and flies that are not yet dead—on a remote Baltic island.

Physics and reproductive medicine collided in a crackle of static electricity and polarized light. The Reproduction Prize honored the late Egyptian urologist Ahmed Shafik, who outfitted male rats in tiny trousers stitched from 100 percent polyester, cotton, wool, or a 50/50 polyester-cotton blend. Shafik discovered that rats wearing pure polyester pants suffered a dramatic drop in sexual activity due to electrostatic potentials generated across the scrotum—a contraceptive effect he subsequently verified in human male volunteers. Meanwhile, Gábor Horváth, Susanne Åkesson, and an international team won the Physics Prize for solving two optical riddles of the insect world: why white-haired horses are the most horsefly-proof horses (their coats scatter unpolarized light, whereas dark horses reflect horizontally polarized light that attracts biting tabanids), and why dragonflies are fatally drawn to polished black tombstones, which mimic the polarized glare of water and trick dragonflies into laying eggs on graves.

Inside the labyrinth of human perception and deception, scientists proved just how easily the brain can be fooled. German neurologists led by Christoph Helmchen and Andreas Sprenger earned the Medicine Prize for showing that if you have a maddening itch on your left forearm, you can relieve it by looking into a mirror positioned at your midline while scratching your right forearm, tricking your visual cortex into soothing the un-scratched limb. Japan's Atsuki Higashiyama and Kohei Adachi took the Perception Prize for investigating 'Matanozoki'—the traditional act of bending over and viewing the world upside down between one's own legs—confirming that inverted posture makes distant landscapes appear smaller and closer. And in the Psychology Prize, Evelyne Debey, Bruno Verschuere, and colleagues interviewed 1,005 subjects aged 6 to 77 to ask how often they lie, before grappling with the philosophical paradox of whether to believe self-reported statistics from prolific liars.

The final trio of prizes aimed a scalpel at modern corporate and cultural pretension. Canadian researchers led by Gordon Pennycook won the Peace Prize for their landmark paper 'On the Reception and Detection of Pseudo-Profound Bullshit,' demonstrating that people who rate randomly generated, grammatically correct buzzword sentences ('Wholeness quiets infinite phenomena') as deeply meaningful score lower in analytic thinking and higher in conspiratorial beliefs. New Zealand and UK scholars Mark Avis, Sarah Forbes, and Shelagh Ferguson claimed the Economics Prize for asking consumers to evaluate the 'brand personality' of ordinary rocks—finding that test subjects eagerly described random stones as 'glamorous,' 'sentimental,' or 'sincere,' thereby exposing the absurdity of corporate brand-personality scales. Finally, the Chemistry Prize was awarded to Volkswagen for solving excessive automobile pollution emissions by electromechanically producing fewer emissions only when the car was being tested.

article_paragraphs: 2017年第27届搞笑诺贝尔奖从铲屎官的日常困惑中提炼出了硬核物理。法国学者马克-安托万·法尔丁凭论文《论猫的流变学》夺得物理学奖：他引入流体力学的“底波拉数”，严谨证明只要给猫咪充足的松弛时间去适应酒杯、鱼缸或纸箱，成年猫就会像液体一样完美填满容器，从而既是固体又是液体。同样研究液体的韩国高中生韩智元则斩获流体动力学奖，他发现端着咖啡倒着走或从上方抓握杯口，能有效抑制步伐引发的液体晃动共振，终结了边走边洒咖啡的难题。

动物王国的饮食与婚恋内幕彻底颠覆了人类三观。日本与巴西学者吉泽和德、费雷拉等人荣获生物学奖，他们在巴西洞穴昆虫中首次发现雌雄生殖器倒置的奇观——雌虫长着带倒刺的阴茎状器官，交配时会伸入雄虫的阴道状体腔内长达数十小时，强行吸取富含营养的精包。巴西学者伊托团队则因营养学奖拉响警报：原本只吸鸟血的毛腿吸血蝠在森林遭侵占后，已开始夜间偷吸人血。而在澳大利亚，经济学奖得主洛克洛夫与格里尔通过实验证实，嗜赌者在抱过活鳄鱼后，会把恐惧带来的心跳加速误判为“手气正旺的兴奋”，从而在老虎机上疯狂加注。

医学与解剖学的镜头对准了从胎儿到老翁的身体奥秘。英国医生希思科特用尺子测量两百多名患者后获解剖学奖，证实人过三十岁后耳朵仍以每年零点二二毫米的速度持续变长，解开了“为什么老爷爷耳朵那么大”的谜题。西班牙产科学奖得主洛佩斯-特伊洪团队发现，把特制微型音箱塞进孕妇阴道内放音乐，胎儿在超声画面下张嘴吐舌头的反应远比隔着肚皮放音乐强烈。瑞士普汉团队则拿下和平奖，证明每天坚持吹奏澳洲原住民乐器迪吉里杜管能锻炼气道肌肉，有效缓解睡眠呼吸暂停与打鼾。
大脑深处的爱憎与自我认知同样耐人寻味。法国鲁瓦耶与蒋涛团队摘得医学奖，利用功能性磁共振成像测出讨厌奶酪的人闻到奶酪味时，大脑负责奖赏的腹侧苍白球竟反转成了表达生理厌恶的开关。意大利罗马大学的马尔蒂尼团队则捧起认知学奖，证明许多同卵双胞胎在看照片时缺乏自我面孔识别优势，常常分不清照片里究竟是自己还是双胞胎手足。

title_en: 2017: The Rheology of Liquid Cats, Crocodile-Holding Gamblers & Sex-Reversed Cave Insects
subtitle_en: The 27th Ceremony: Proving Felines Are Both Solid and Liquid, and Treating Sleep Apnea with a Didgeridoo
article_paragraphs_en: The 27th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony distilled hard-core rheology out of the internet's favorite feline memes. French physicist Marc-Antoine Fardin won the Physics Prize for his paper 'On the Rheology of Cats,' which deployed the dimensionless Deborah number—the ratio of a material's relaxation time to the observation time—to answer whether a cat can be both a solid and a liquid. Fardin demonstrated that while a cat observed over a split second bounces like an elastic solid, an adult cat given a few minutes to settle into a wine glass, sink basin, or shoebox flows to fill every corner like a true liquid. A fellow pioneer of everyday fluid mechanics, South Korean high-school student Jiwon Han, captured the Fluid Dynamics Prize for proving that walking backward while carrying a cup of coffee—or gripping the rim from above like a claw—dampens the biomechanically induced sloshing resonance that normally spills coffee over your shoes.

Across the animal kingdom, discoveries in diet, anatomy, and risk-taking turned conventional wisdom inside out. Japanese, Brazilian, and Swiss biologists Kazunori Yoshizawa, Rodrigo Ferreira, Yoshitaka Kamimura, and Charles Lienhard won the Biology Prize for discovering a cave-dwelling insect genus (*Neotrogla*) in which the female possesses an elaborate, barbed penis-like organ (*gynosome*) that penetrates the male's vagina-like chamber for up to 70 hours to forcibly extract nutritious seminal gifts. In Brazil, Fernanda Ito, Enrico Bernard, and Rodrigo Torres earned the Nutrition Prize for the first DNA-verified report that hairy-legged vampire bats—previously thought to feed exclusively on birds—have started sneaking human blood meals at night due to deforestation. Meanwhile, in Australia, Matthew Rockloff and Nancy Greer claimed the Economics Prize by having volunteers hold a live one-meter saltwater crocodile just before playing an electronic slot machine, revealing that problem gamblers misattribute terror-induced physiological arousal as 'lucky excitement' and place significantly larger bets.

Clinical medicine and anatomy zoomed in on the human body from womb to old age. British general practitioner James Heathcote received the Anatomy Prize for his classic study 'Why Do Old Men Have Big Ears?', measuring 206 patients to confirm that human ears continue elongating after age 30 at a steady clip of 0.22 millimeters per year—adding a full centimeter over half a century. Spanish obstetricians led by Marisa López-Teijón won the Obstetrics Prize for proving via ultrasound that a developing fetus responds with vigorous mouth-opening and tongue-sticking movements when music is broadcast electromechanically inside the mother's vagina (via their patented 'Babypod' speaker), whereas music played against the mother's abdomen barely registers. And a Swiss-led team headed by Milo Puhan and patient-inventor Alex Suarez won the Peace Prize for a randomized controlled trial proving that practicing the Australian Aboriginal didgeridoo strengthens upper-airway muscles and significantly reduces obstructive sleep apnea and disruptive snoring.

The final two prizes peered directly into the human brain to examine self-recognition and culinary revulsion. French and British neuroscientists Jean-Pierre Royet, Tao Jiang, and colleagues won the Medicine Prize for sliding cheese-haters into an fMRI scanner and discovering that the smell and sight of pungent cheese deactivate and repurpose the ventral pallidum—a core brain reward structure—into an active circuit of disgust. Finally, Italian and Spanish researchers led by Matteo Martini and Salvatore Maria Aglioti took the Cognition Prize for demonstrating that many identical twins lack the normal visual self-face recognition advantage, frequently struggling to tell whether a photograph shows their own face or that of their twin.

article_paragraphs: 2018年第28届搞笑诺贝尔奖把医疗诊室搬上了游乐场与自家马桶。美国泌尿科医生米切尔与瓦廷格斩获医学奖：受患者启发，他们用硅胶打印出装有尿液和三颗真结石的仿真肾脏，揣进背包去奥兰多迪士尼乐园连坐二十趟“巨雷山铁路”过山车，证实坐车尾排石率高达六成以上，远胜车头。同样追求极致的日本医生堀内朗则独揽医学教育奖，他坐在椅子上左手握操纵杆、右手把细口径结肠镜塞进自己肛门，连做四次坐姿自我肠镜，写出了令人肃然起敬的无痛自检指南。

在生殖医学与古人类食谱的角落里，科学家们算出了最精明的账目。美国医生巴里、布兰克和布瓦洛凭借1980年的经典研究摘得生殖医学奖：他们发明了廉价的“邮票勃起测试法”，只需睡前在男性阴茎上围一圈连体邮票，次日清晨看邮票齿孔是否被撑断，就能轻松鉴别器质性与心理性阳痿。英国考古学家詹姆斯·科尔则捧走营养学奖，他细致核算人体各器官的热量表后证明，吃人肉所能获取的卡路里远低于猛犸象、野猪甚至马肉，说明旧石器时代古人类同类相食绝非为了充饥，而是出于文化仪式动机。

感官与日常行为实验室里同样好戏连台。瑞典与德国的贝歇尔团队荣获生物学奖，证实哪怕只有一只雌性果蝇掉进葡萄酒杯，它释放的微量性信息素也足以让品酒大师仅凭嗅觉就当场识破。葡萄牙文物修复专家罗芒等人拿下化学奖，通过实验证明人类口水中的淀粉酶确实是清洁十八世纪镀金雕像与古画脏污表面的绝佳去污剂。而在动物园玻璃幕墙两侧，人类学奖得主佩尔松团队观察到，黑猩猩模仿人类游客拍手、敲窗和鬼脸的频率与水准，与人类游客模仿黑猩猩的表现不相上下。
现代职场、交通与消费生活的痛点在最后三项大奖中展露无遗。加拿大与中国的梁瀚予、廉慧文等学者斩获经济学奖，发现受恶毒上司欺凌的员工对着写有老板名字的巫毒娃娃扎针，能显著平复屈辱感、重获心理正义。西班牙阿隆索团队因系统测量司机开车时喊叫与咒骂的路怒症行为而获和平奖；澳大利亚布莱克勒团队则耗时七年拿下文学奖，用铁证道出了全人类的共同习惯——无论复杂电子产品功能多繁多，绝大多数人都绝不看使用说明书。

title_en: 2018: Kidney-Stone Roller Coasters, Boss Voodoo Dolls & Self-Administered Colonoscopies
subtitle_en: The 28th Ceremony: From Postage-Stamp Erection Tests to Why Nobody Ever Reads the Instruction Manual
article_paragraphs_en: The 28th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony relocated medical science from the sterile hospital ward to the amusement park and the doctor's own chair. American osteopathic urologists Marc Mitchell and David Wartinger captured the Medicine Prize after patients repeatedly reported passing kidney stones following rides on Disney World's Big Thunder Mountain Railroad. To test the claim rigorously, the duo 3D-printed a transparent silicone renal model modeled on an actual patient's CT scan, filled it with urine and three real kidney stones of varying sizes, tucked it into a backpack, and rode the roller coaster 20 times—proving that sitting in the rear car yielded a whopping 63.89 percent stone-passage rate compared to just 16.67 percent in the front seat. Matching their dedication, Japanese gastroenterologist Akira Horiuchi won the Medical Education Prize for sitting upright in a chair, holding a small-caliber colonoscope controller in his left hand, and inserting the tube into his own rectum with his right hand four separate times to demonstrate the comfort of seated self-colonoscopy.

Ingenious frugal diagnostics and Paleolithic calorie-counting took home two more honors. American urologists John Barry, Bruce Blank, and Michel Boileau won the Reproductive Medicine Prize for their classic 1980 paper 'Nocturnal Penile Tumescence Monitoring With Stamps,' showing that wrapping a ring of joined postage stamps snugly around a sleeping man's penis overnight—and checking in the morning whether the perforations have been snapped—reliably distinguishes organic impotence from psychogenic erectile dysfunction at a fraction of sleep-lab costs. Meanwhile, British archaeologist James Cole earned the Nutrition Prize for calculating a comprehensive nutritional table of the human body, proving that a Paleolithic cannibalism diet provides significantly fewer calories than hunting mammoths, woolly rhinos, wild boars, or horses, and thus prehistoric cannibalism was likely driven by social or ritual motives rather than simple hunger.

Sensory acuity, conservation chemistry, and primate mimicry sparkled in the natural sciences. An international team led by Paul Becher, Sebastien Lebreton, and Peter Witzgall won the Biology Prize for demonstrating that professional wine experts can reliably detect by smell alone whether a single female fruit fly (*Drosophila melanogaster*) has fallen into a glass of wine, thanks to a nanogram-level sex pheromone (*Z4-11Al*) secreted by the female fly that ruins the bouquet. Portuguese conservation scientists Paula Romão, Adília Alarcão, and the late César Viana received the Chemistry Prize for quantifying what mothers and art restorers have long suspected: human saliva—powered by alpha-amylase enzymes—is a remarkably effective cleaning agent for dirty 18th-century gilded sculptures and painted surfaces. And at Furuvik Zoo, Anthropology Prize winners Tomas Persson, Gabriela-Alina Sauciuc, and Elainie Madsen documented that chimpanzees imitate human visitors' claps, window knocks, and grimaces just as frequently and skillfully as humans imitate the apes.

Finally, the frustrations of modern work, traffic, and consumer electronics received overdue scientific validation. Researchers Lindie Hanyu Liang, Douglas Brown, Huiwen Lian, and colleagues won the Economics Prize for proving that employees mistreated by an abusive supervisor feel a restored sense of psychological justice after sticking pins, pliers, and fire into a virtual Voodoo doll labeled with their boss's initials. Spanish traffic researchers led by Francisco Alonso earned the Peace Prize for systematically measuring how often—and why—motorists shout and curse behind the wheel. Rounding out the ceremony, Australian and UK ergonomists Thea Blackler, Rafael Gomez, Vesna Popovic, and M. Helen Thompson won the Literature Prize for their seven-year study 'Life Is Too Short to RTFM,' confirming experimentally that most people never read the instruction manual no matter how complicated a product is.

article_paragraphs: 2019年第29届搞笑诺贝尔奖见证了流体力学界的“梅开二度”。继2015年发现哺乳动物二十一秒排尿定律后，美籍华裔学者杨佩良与胡立德团队再度斩获物理学奖，解开了澳洲袋熊拉出正方体便便之谜：原来袋熊大肠末端软硬厚度不一，通过周期性收缩将粪便塑造成棱角分明的立方体，方便堆在岩石上标记领地而不滚落。中国与新加坡学者孔令军、帕特雷克团队则荣获生物学奖，发现被磁化的死蟑螂与活蟑螂表现截然不同，死蟑螂由于体内细胞质硬化，磁性维持时间竟长达近五十个小时。

人体的分泌物与温度在科学家眼中全是宝藏。日本学者渡边茂团队摘得化学奖，他们在三十五年前让三十名五岁孩童把嚼碎的食物连同口水吐进杯子称重，精确算出五岁小孩每天约分泌五百毫升唾液——颁奖礼现场，当年吐口水的儿子们已长大成人，亲自上台陪父亲领奖。法国学者米约塞与本古迪法荣获解剖学奖，通过给法国邮递员贴温度传感器，证实无论裸体还是穿裤子，人类左侧睾丸的温度总是显著高于右侧。沙特、英国和美国学者组成的团队则捧起和平奖，量化证实抓挠脚踝止痒带来的快感远胜前臂与背部。
医学与工程学的跨界脑洞令人忍俊不禁。意大利学者加卢斯荣获医学奖，证明常吃披萨能显著降低患癌与急性心梗风险，但前提是披萨必须在意大利制作并吃下。美国训犬师普赖尔与麦基翁夺得医学教育奖，她们把训练小狗和海豚的“响片训练法”引入手术室，外科新手每做好一个动作就按响片给予正向激励，效果远超传统教学。伊朗工程师法拉赫巴赫什则凭全自动婴儿洗屁股兼换尿布机拿下了工程学奖。
金钱与微笑的真相在最后两项大奖中浮出水面。荷兰与土耳其的沃斯父子及格迪克斩获经济学奖，把各国纸币泡进菌液测试后，发现采用聚合物塑料基材的罗马尼亚列伊纸币最擅长把金黄色葡萄球菌和大肠杆菌传给数钱的人。最令人感佩的则是德国心理学家弗里茨·斯特拉克：他在1988年发现咬住笔杆迫使嘴角上扬会让人更快乐，却在近三十年后坦然认可跨实验室重复实验推翻了自己的结论，凭这份自我纠错的科学胸怀赢得心理学奖。

title_en: 2019: Wombat Cubed Poo, French Postmen's Scrotal Temperatures & Clicker-Trained Surgeons
subtitle_en: The 29th Ceremony: Authentic Italian Pizza for Longevity and an Automated Baby Diaper-Washer
article_paragraphs_en: The 29th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony witnessed a triumphant return by the reigning monarchs of biological fluid mechanics. Four years after winning the 2015 Physics Prize for the 21-second mammalian urination law, Patricia Yang and David Hu—joined by Scott Carver, Alexander Lee, Miles Chan, Alynn Martin, and Ashley Edwards—captured their second Physics Prize for discovering how and why Australian wombats produce cube-shaped poo. Dissecting roadkill wombats, the team discovered that the final eight percent of a wombat's intestine has non-uniform elasticity—two stiff grooves alternating with two flexible regions—which rhythmically compresses drying feces into sharp-cornered two-centimeter cubes so wombats can stack them on rocks as territorial cairns without the droppings rolling away. Equally magnetic in the Biology Prize, Ling-Jun Kong, Herbert Crepaz, Tomasz Paterek, and colleagues magnetized live and dead American cockroaches, finding that while live roaches demagnetize in about 50 minutes as magnetic particles stir inside glassy cytoplasm, dead magnetized cockroaches stay magnetic for nearly 50 hours.

Bodily secretions, thermal asymmetries, and the topography of pleasure dominated the physiological prizes. Japanese dental scientist Shigeru Watanabe and his colleagues won the Chemistry Prize for a painstaking 1995 study in which 30 five-year-old children chewed through meals and spat every mouthful into collection cups so researchers could weigh the moisture difference, proving a typical five-year-old produces about 500 milliliters of saliva per day—and at Harvard, Watanabe's now-middle-aged sons, who served as the original spitting subjects 35 years ago, joined him onstage! In France, Roger Mieusset and Bourras Bengoudifa won the Anatomy Prize for wiring naked and clothed French postmen with thermal probes, proving that the left testicle is consistently warmer than the right testicle. And an international dermatology team led by Ghada A. bin Saif, Francis McGlone, and Gil Yosipovitch took the Peace Prize for rubbing cowhage spicules onto volunteers' forearms, backs, and ankles, proving that scratching an itchy ankle delivers the highest pleasure ratings of all.

Cross-disciplinary medical and engineering ingenuity sparked roars of laughter. Italian epidemiologist Silvano Gallus earned the Medicine Prize for three papers showing that regular pizza consumption protects against digestive tract cancers and acute myocardial infarction—with the crucial caveat that the pizza must be baked and eaten in Italy. American animal-training pioneer Karen Pryor and Theresa McKeon won the Medical Education Prize for teaching orthopedic surgery residents how to tie knots and drill bone with acoustic 'clicker training' originally developed for dolphins and puppies, achieving significantly higher precision than conventional demonstration teaching. Meanwhile, Iranian engineer Iman Farahbakhsh won the Engineering Prize for patenting an automated infant washer and diaper-changing machine that straps a baby inside a dishwasher-like cabinet to strip, wash, dry, and re-diaper the infant automatically.

Finally, filthy lucre and scientific humility closed out the night. Dutch and Turkish researchers Habip Gedik, Timothy Voss, and Andreas Voss (a father-and-son duo) won the Economics Prize for spiking banknotes from around the world with MRSA, *E. coli*, and VRE bacteria, discovering that polymer-based Romanian Leu notes were the most effective currency at transmitting dangerous pathogens to human fingers. And the Psychology Prize honored Germany's Fritz Strack, who famously reported in 1988 that holding a pen between one's teeth forces a smile that makes cartoons seem funnier—only to participate in and graciously accept a massive 2016 multi-lab replication study proving the effect did not hold up, earning a standing ovation for scientific self-correction.

article_paragraphs: 2020年第30届搞笑诺贝尔奖首次移师线上，诞生了中国观众最熟悉的传奇大奖。管理学奖颁给广西南宁五名层层转包的杀手——奚广安收下雇主两百万元买凶巨款后，留下一百万转包给莫天祥，莫天祥转包杨康生，杨康生又转包杨广生，最后以十万元转包给凌显四。经四道中间商雁过拔毛，凌显四觉得为十万块钱杀人坐牢太亏，干脆约暗杀对象在咖啡馆商量演场“假死戏”交差，最终五人全部获刑，全链条无人伤亡。和平奖则颁给印巴两国政府：两国外交官半夜偷偷去按对方家门铃，再趁开门前拔腿狂奔，把外交博弈玩成孩童恶作剧。

动物与材料实验室里上演着声音与温度的魔幻剧。奥地利与日本的雷伯、西村刚团队斩获声学奖，把一条雌性扬子鳄关进充满氦氧混合气的密闭舱内咆哮，凭变调的高频叫声首次证实鳄鱼也拥有声道共振结构。澳大利亚学者马克西莫夫与波托茨基获物理学奖，把用酒精灌醉的活蚯蚓放在低音炮上高频振动，观察到蚯蚓表面荡漾出如同液体的法拉第驻波。美国学者埃伦团队则夺得材料科学奖：为验证“因纽特老人用冰冻大便磨刀杀狗”的传说，他们连续八天吃高蛋白饮食并把粪便冻在零下二十度塑形成刀，结果粪便刀一碰猪皮就当场融化。
人类的心理怪癖在显微镜下无所遁形。美国学者维特荣获昆虫学奖，调查发现许多整天抓蟑螂毛虫的昆虫学家竟极度害怕蜘蛛——只因蜘蛛比六条腿的昆虫多了两条腿。荷兰与比利时的武林克团队摘得医学奖，正式定义了听到别人咀嚼、吞咽或呼吸声就会暴怒崩溃的“恐音症”。美加学者贾科敏与鲁尔则捧起心理学奖，证实自恋狂往往拥有更浓密且精心修剪的眉毛，哪怕遮住全脸只看眉毛也能一眼认出自恋者。

宏观数据与现实政治在最后两项大奖中交织出深刻讽刺。英国沃特金斯领衔的跨国团队获经济学奖，发现国民收入不平等越严重的国家，伴侣嘴对嘴接吻越频繁。而医学教育奖则颁给了巴西博索纳罗、英国约翰逊、印度莫迪、墨西哥奥夫拉多尔、白俄罗斯卢卡申科、美国特朗普、土耳其埃尔多安、俄罗斯普京与土库曼斯坦别尔德穆哈梅多夫九国领导人，表彰他们利用新冠疫情向世界证明：政客对人类生死存亡的直接影响，远比科学家和医生更加立竿见影。

title_en: 2020: China's Five-Tier Subcontracting Hitmen, Helium-Voiced Alligators & Frozen Feces Knives
subtitle_en: The 30th Ceremony: From Doorbell-Ditching Diplomats to Spider-Fearing Entomologists
article_paragraphs_en: Forced online for the first time by a global pandemic, the 30th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize Ceremony delivered one of the most hilarious case studies in corporate outsourcing history. The Management Prize went to five professional hitmen in Guangxi, China—Xi Guang-An, Mo Tian-Xiang, Yang Kang-Sheng, Yang Guang-Sheng, and Ling Xian-Si. Hired for 2 million yuan to murder a business rival, Xi Guang-An pocketed half and subcontracted the hit for 1 million yuan to Mo Tian-Xiang, who subcontracted it to Yang Kang-Sheng, who subcontracted it to Yang Guang-Sheng, who finally offered a measly 100,000 yuan to Ling Xian-Si. Concluding that 100,000 yuan was far too little pay for a murder sentence, Ling invited the intended victim to a café and proposed staging a fake kidnapping photo instead—whereupon the target reported the plot to police, landing all five middlemen in prison without a single scratch inflicted. In a similar spirit of petty escalation, the Peace Prize went to the governments of India and Pakistan for having their diplomats surreptitiously ring each other's doorbells in the middle of the night and sprint away before anyone could answer.

Laboratories of acoustics, physics, and materials science staged surreal experiments in sound and temperature. An international team including Stephan Reber, Takeshi Nishimura, Judith Janisch, Mark Robertson, and Tecumseh Fitch won the Acoustics Prize for inducing a female Chinese alligator to bellow inside an airtight chamber filled with helium-oxygen gas ('heliox'); the resulting high-pitched resonance shifts proved that crocodilians use vocal-tract formants to advertise body size just like mammals. In Australia, Ivan Maksymov and Andrey Pototsky earned the Physics Prize for sedating living earthworms with vodka and vibrating them on a subwoofer speaker to excite liquid-like Faraday standing waves along their bodies. And anthropologist Metin Eren, Michelle Bebber, and colleagues won the Materials Science Prize for testing the famous ethnographic legend of an Inuit elder who supposedly crafted a knife from his own frozen feces to butcher a dog: after eating an Arctic high-protein diet for eight days and molding knives from their own poop at minus 20 degrees Celsius, the team proved that frozen fecal blades immediately melt into brown streaks upon touching warm pig hide.

Human phobias, auditory rage, and facial cues were laid bare under the psychological microscope. Retired American entomologist Richard Vetter won the Entomology Prize for surveying fellow bug scientists and proving that a surprising number of professional entomologists are terrified of spiders—primarily because spiders have eight legs rather than six, violating the six-legged comfort zone of insect researchers. Dutch and Belgian psychiatrists Nienke Vulink, Damiaan Denys, and Arnoud van Loon received the Medicine Prize for formally diagnosing and treating *misophonia*, the intense rage and distress triggered by hearing other people chew, slurp, or breathe. Meanwhile, psychologists Miranda Giacomin and Nicholas Rule earned the Psychology Prize for demonstrating that grandiose narcissists can be accurately identified from photographs of their eyebrows alone, since narcissists unconsciously maintain thicker, more distinctively groomed brows to maximize recognition.

Macroeconomic romance and pandemic politics brought the milestone 30th ceremony to a biting crescendo. A multinational team led by Scotland's Christopher Watkins won the Economics Prize for surveying 13 nations and discovering that countries with higher national income inequality exhibit a significantly higher frequency of mouth-to-mouth kissing between romantic partners. Finally, the Medical Education Prize was jointly awarded to nine national leaders—Jair Bolsonaro of Brazil, Boris Johnson of the UK, Narendra Modi of India, Andrés Manuel López Obrador of Mexico, Alexander Lukashenko of Belarus (his second Ig Nobel Prize!), Donald Trump of the USA, Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey, Vladimir Putin of Russia, and Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow of Turkmenistan—for using the Covid-19 pandemic to teach the world that politicians can have a more immediate effect on life and death than scientists and doctors can.

article_paragraphs: 2021年9月9日，第31届搞笑诺贝尔奖在云端爆笑揭晓。最吸睛的交通运输奖中，康奈尔大学的罗宾·拉德克利夫与马克·贾戈、彼得·莫克尔等十三位学者为拯救非洲濒危黑犀牛，真的用直升机把十二头麻醉黑犀牛四脚朝天吊在半空做实验，证实倒挂飞行时犀牛的心肺通气与血氧指标比担架侧卧更健康。动物研究同样精彩：瑞典学者苏珊·舍茨、罗伯特·埃克伦德与约斯特·范德维耶系统解析了猫咪对人发出的呼噜、啾啾、颤音、喵喵与咆哮等十余种声学调门，凭“喵星语”研究斩获生物学奖；小约翰·马尔伦南、罗杰·格罗特豪斯、查尔斯·哈蒙德与杰伊·拉姆丁则凭利用杀虫剂在幽闭潜艇内灭绝蟑螂的方案捧走昆虫学奖。

物理学奖与动力学奖在人行道上演了一出“左右互搏”的双簧戏。亚历山德罗·科尔贝塔、贾斯珀·梅乌森、李忠民、罗伯托·本齐与费德里科·托斯基在火车站追踪数万名旅客，建模解释了为什么行人摩肩接踵却不会频繁相撞，摘得物理学奖；日本学者村上久与克劳迪奥·费利奇亚尼、西山雄大、西成活裕则反证：只要有人边走边看手机，人群双向预判机制就会瞬间崩溃并引发相撞，拿下动力学奖。西班牙与伊朗学者莱拉·萨塔里、阿尔芭·吉列恩、安赫拉·维达尔-韦尔杜和曼努埃尔·波尔卡尔满大街刮取各国路面上被踩扁的风干口香糖，通过基因测序绘制出黏胶里的细菌演替图谱，荣获生态学奖。

人体气味、快感与政坛研究更是脑洞大开。约尔格·维克、乔纳森·威廉姆斯等十位学者分析电影院空气，证实观众呼出的异戊二烯等挥发性气体能可靠反映银幕上的暴力、性、吸毒与脏话程度，甚至可用来给电影做年龄分级，夺得化学奖。奥尔蔡·杰姆·布卢特、达雷·奥拉多昆、布尔卡德·利珀特与拉尔夫·霍亨伯格为情侣测量鼻腔气流，证明性高潮通鼻塞的效果媲美减充血药物，斩获医学奖；伊桑·贝塞里斯、史蒂文·纳勒韦与大卫·卡里尔用披羊毛的环氧树脂模拟下巴做落锤实验，证实浓密胡须能吸收重拳冲击以保护面部，捧走和平奖。帕夫洛·布拉瓦茨基则用算法扫描后苏联国家政客脸部照片估算体重指数，发现政客越肥胖往往意味着该国腐败越严重，拿下了辛辣的经济学奖。

title_en: Upside-Down Airborne Rhinos, Cinema Odor Ratings, and the Pugilism Beard Hypothesis
subtitle_en: From sidewalk chewing-gum microbiomes to portly politicians and pedestrian near-misses, the 2021 virtual ceremony turned everyday oddities into high science
article_paragraphs_en: On September 9, 2021, the 31st First Annual Ig Nobel Prize ceremony streamed online for the second pandemic year, celebrating ten studies that made the world laugh and then think. Stealing the spotlight in the Transportation Prize was a thirteen-member international team led by Cornell University wildlife veterinarian Robin Radcliffe alongside Mark Jago, Peter Morkel, Estelle Morkel, Pierre du Preez, Piet Beytell, Birgit Kotting, Bakker Manuel, Jan Hendrik du Preez, Michele Miller, Julia Felippe, Stephen Parry, and Robin Gleed. To ensure conservationists were not harming endangered black rhinoceroses in Namibia when airlifting them by helicopter over rough terrain, the team suspended twelve tranquilized rhinos upside-down by their feet from a crane. Astonishingly, hanging upside-down improved the rhinos' blood oxygen levels and reduced pulmonary dead space compared to lying on their sides on a stretcher. Animal communication and pest control also shone: Sweden's Susanne Schötz, Robert Eklund, and Joost van de Weijer won the Biology Prize for acoustically decoding the purring, chirping, chattering, trilling, tweedling, murmuring, meowing, moaning, squeaking, hissing, yowling, howling, and growling that domestic cats use to converse with humans, while Americans John Mulrennan, Jr., Roger Grothaus, Charles Hammond, and Jay Lamdin took the Entomology Prize for their 1971 U.S. Navy study on eradicating cockroaches aboard submarines using dichlorvos aerosols.

On city sidewalks, the Physics Prize and the Kinetics Prize staged a hilarious scientific duet on pedestrian traffic. Alessandro Corbetta, Jasper Meeusen, Chung-min Lee, Roberto Benzi, and Federico Toschi earned the Physics Prize after tracking hundreds of thousands of commuters in a Dutch train station to model why pedestrians do not constantly collide with one another. Answering the obvious follow-up question, Hisashi Murakami, Claudio Feliciani, Yuta Nishiyama, and Katsuhiro Nishinari captured the Kinetics Prize by demonstrating why pedestrians sometimes do collide: when even a few walkers stare at smartphones, the subtle visual anticipation that allows human crowds to self-organize into smooth lanes abruptly collapses. Meanwhile, beneath those pedestrians' shoes, Ecology Prize laureates Leila Satari, Alba Guillén, Àngela Vidal-Verdú, and Manuel Porcar scraped wads of discarded chewing gum off pavements across five countries, using genetic sequencing to map how oral bacteria gradually give way to hardy environmental microbes trapped in the sticky rubber.

Human physiology, pugilism, and political portliness rounded out a banner year. Jörg Wicker, Nicolas Krauter, Bettina Derstroff, Christof Stönner, Efstratios Bourtsoukidis, Achim Edtbauer, Jochen Wulf, Thomas Klüpfel, Stefan Kramer, and Jonathan Williams won the Chemistry Prize for sampling movie theater air with mass spectrometers, proving that volatile organic compounds like isoprene exhaled by tense moviegoers reliably indicate the levels of violence, sex, antisocial behavior, drug use, and bad language on screen. In the Medicine Prize, Olcay Cem Bulut, Dare Oladokun, Burkard Lippert, and Ralph Hohenberger equipped eighteen couples with portable rhinometers and demonstrated that sexual orgasms clear nasal congestion just as effectively as commercial decongestant sprays for up to an hour. Peace Prize winners Ethan Beseris, Steven Naleway, and David Carrier tested the 'pugilism hypothesis' by dropping weights onto epoxy bone composites wrapped in sheepskin fleece, showing that a full beard absorbs 37 percent more impact energy to protect facial bones from punches. Finally, economist Pavlo Blavatskyy clinched the Economics Prize by running computer-vision BMI estimates on portraits of 299 post-Soviet cabinet ministers, revealing that the waistlines of a nation's politicians serve as a remarkably accurate barometer of state corruption.

article_paragraphs: 2022年9月15日，第32届搞笑诺贝尔奖在云端揭幕。物理学奖联合授予弗兰克·费什以及袁志明、陈明璐、贾来兵、姬春艳与阿蒂拉·因杰吉克团队，他们从代谢与水波动力学入手，发现排在母鸭身后的小鸭子不仅能踩在尾波波峰上“乘浪”化阻力为推力，还能像接力棒一样“传浪”实现全队节能。工程类奖项同样妙趣横生：瑞典工程师马格努斯·根斯用上百片橡胶圆盘与钢索拼装出逼真的驼鹿碰撞测试假人，帮助车企测试高速撞上驼鹿时的安全性，荣获安全工程奖；日本学者松崎元、大内一雄、上原胜、上野义雪与井村五郎则通过实验测算出人们拧转不同直径柱状旋钮时，从两指捏合切换到五指抓握的最优效率规律，捧走工程学奖。

生物与医学得主将目光投向了生命体最尴尬或最温柔的角落。巴西学者索利玛丽·加西亚-埃尔南德斯与格劳科·马查多斩获生物学奖，他们发现蝎子遇险自断尾巴保命时会把尾端的肛门一并丢掉，导致终生无法排便而严重便秘，但断尾雄蝎在被憋死前的数月里依然能四处交配。波兰学者马尔钦·亚辛斯基、埃米利安·斯纳尔斯基等九位医生在医学奖中献上暖心良方：接受毒性化疗的患者只要用吃冰淇淋代替传统含冰块冷冻疗法，就能显著减少口腔黏膜炎副作用。埃莉什卡·普罗哈兹科娃与玛莉丝卡·克雷特等人则在相亲实验中发现，初次见面的男女一旦彼此心动，两人的心率就会神奇地同步跳动，摘得应用心脏病学奖。

人文与社科奖项更是刀刀见血。埃里克·马丁内斯、弗朗西斯·莫利卡与爱德华·吉布森剖析法律文件，指出法条晦涩难懂并非因为概念高深，纯粹源于糟糕的句式写作，拿下文学奖；彼得·德斯梅特与尼古拉斯·赫尔穆特凭对古玛雅陶器上“仪式性灌肠场景”的跨学科考证荣膺艺术史奖。中国学者武俊辉与保罗·范朗格等十一位学者构建数学算法，推演出八卦传播者何时该说真话、何时该撒谎，夺得和平奖；意大利学者亚历山德罗·普卢基诺、阿莱西奥·比翁多与安德烈亚·拉皮萨达则用数学模型无情证明：世俗的成功往往不属于最有才华的人，而是属于最幸运的人，这也让他们生涯第二次捧起搞笑诺奖奖杯。

title_en: Wave-Riding Ducklings, Constipated Scorpions, and the Swedish Moose Crash-Test Dummy
subtitle_en: Synchronized blind-date heartbeats, chemotherapy ice cream, and a mathematical proof that luck beats talent every time
article_paragraphs_en: On September 15, 2022, the 32nd First Annual Ig Nobel Prize ceremony celebrated ten triumphs of delightfully eccentric curiosity. The Physics Prize was awarded jointly to American biologist Frank Fish and to naval hydrodynamics researchers Zhi-Ming Yuan, Minglu Chen, Laibing Jia, Chunyan Ji, and Atilla Incecik for explaining how ducklings swim in formation. By placing ducklings in a swim flume and modeling the fluid mechanics of their mother's wake, the researchers discovered that the first duckling surfs the mother's wave crest—converting wave drag into forward thrust—while trailing ducklings act as 'wave passers' that relay hydrodynamic energy down the entire line without attenuation. Ingenious engineering also took center stage: Sweden's Magnus Gens won the Safety Engineering Prize for constructing a realistic moose crash-test dummy out of stacked high-density rubber discs and steel cables so automakers could design windshields capable of surviving high-speed moose collisions. Meanwhile, Japanese ergonomists Gen Matsuzaki, Kazuo Ohuchi, Masaru Uehara, Yoshiyuki Ueno, and Goro Imura captured the Engineering Prize for filming volunteers turning cylindrical knobs of varying diameters to determine the exact thresholds where human hands switch from a two-finger pinch to three-, four-, and five-finger grips.

In biology and medicine, researchers explored romance, chemotherapy comfort, and extreme invertebrate anatomy. Brazilian zoologists Solimary García-Hernández and Glauco Machado earned the Biology Prize for investigating how constipation affects the mating prospects of scorpions. When a scorpion sheds its tail to escape a predator, it also loses its anus, rendering it permanently unable to defecate; yet constipated males still scramble to find mates before perishing months later from toxic buildup. Poland's Marcin Jasiński, Martyna Maciejewska, Anna Brodziak, Michał Górka, Kamila Skwierawska, Wiesław Jędrzejczak, Agnieszka Tomaszewska, Grzegorz Basak, and Emilian Snarski won the Medicine Prize for proving that giving cancer patients hospital-cafeteria ice cream instead of traditional ice chips during toxic high-dose melphalan chemotherapy dramatically reduces painful oral mucositis. And in the Applied Cardiology Prize, Eliska Prochazkova, Elio Sjak-Shie, Friederike Behrens, Daniel Lindh, and Mariska Kret wired singles into blind-date booths at festivals, proving that when two strangers feel mutual romantic attraction, their heart rates and skin conductance synchronize.

Humanities and social science laureates delivered equally sharp insights into human folly. Cognitive scientists Eric Martínez, Francis Mollica, and Edward Gibson won the Literature Prize by proving that legal documents are maddeningly difficult to read not because of complex legal concepts, but because lawyers stuff center-embedded clauses, passive verbs, and archaic jargon into every sentence. Art History Prize winners Peter de Smet and Nicholas Hellmuth were honored for their classic multidisciplinary study of ritual hallucinogenic enema scenes painted on ancient Maya pottery. In the Peace Prize, Junhui Wu, Szabolcs Számadó, Pat Barclay, Bianca Beersma, Terence Dores Cruz, Sergio Lo Iacono, Annika Nieper, Kim Peters, Wojtek Przepiorka, Leo Tiokhin, and Paul Van Lange developed a mathematical algorithm showing gossipers exactly when to tell the truth and when to lie based on fitness interdependence. Finally, Italian physicists Alessandro Pluchino, Alessio Emanuele Biondo, and Andrea Rapisarda—earning Pluchino and Rapisarda's second Ig Nobel—won the Economics Prize for demonstrating mathematically via agent-based simulations why extreme success in life goes almost never to the most talented individuals, but overwhelmingly to the luckiest.

article_paragraphs: 2023年9月14日，第33届搞笑诺贝尔奖将科学家的猎奇精神推向了哥特又赛博的新高度。美国莱斯大学的叶德斐、刘震、阿努普·拉贾潘、特雷弗·下楠与丹尼尔·普雷斯顿斩获机械工程奖，他们巧妙利用蜘蛛步足靠液压伸展、死后自然蜷缩的生理构造，将针头插进死狼蛛前体并粘牢充放空气，操控八条腿张合抓起超过自身体重一点三倍的物体，开创了“死灵机器人学”。公共卫生奖同样令人虎躯一震：斯坦福大学的朴升珉发明了集成尿液分析试纸、排便计算机视觉系统与“菊纹识别摄像头”的斯坦福智能马桶，靠扫描每位用户独一无二的肛门纹路来绑定个人排泄物健康监测。

人体解剖与自然感官领域尽显学者们的执着。加州大学的克里斯汀·范与娜塔莎·梅辛科夫斯卡等八人仔细清点遗体鼻毛，证实人类左鼻孔平均长有120根鼻毛、右鼻孔约112根，摘得医学奖；日本明治大学的宫下芳明与中村裕美发明通电筷子与吸管，用微弱电流刺激舌尖改变食物味道并凭空增强咸味，拿下营养学奖；英国学者扬·扎拉谢维奇则撰文解释为什么许多地质学家和古生物学家喜欢舔石头——因为唾液湿润表面比放大镜更能看清矿物与微体化石纹理，荣获化学与地质学奖。西班牙学者别伊托·费尔南德斯·卡斯特罗、贝阿特丽斯·莫里尼奥-卡瓦利多等九人通宵监测海岸，发现凤尾鱼群夜间大规模交配产卵的剧烈游动足以搅动并加速海洋水体混合，捧走物理学奖。

大脑认知与群体心理奖项更让人会心一笑。克里斯·穆兰、妮可·贝尔、阿基拉·奥康纳等人让受试者把同一个简单单词重复抄写无数遍，成功在实验室里诱发出看着熟词却感到无比陌生的“旧事如新症”，夺得文学奖；玛丽亚·何塞·托雷斯-普里奥里斯与阿道夫·加西亚等人扫描倒着说话高手的大脑，揭开音节逆序编码的神经活动奥秘，获颁传播学奖。香港大学的谭茵茵、陈自强与维南德·范蒂尔堡等人系统证实老师讲课无聊会传染给学生、且学生课前预期无聊会让课堂加倍无聊，摘得教育学奖；而心理学大师斯坦利·米尔格拉姆、伦纳德·比克曼与劳伦斯·伯科威茨在城市街头安排托儿抬头看天、测试多少路人会驻足跟风仰望的经典从众实验，则赢得了心理学奖。
