title_en: Necrobotic Spider Grippers, the Anal-Print Smart Toilet, and Why Geologists Lick Rocks
subtitle_en: Electrified chopsticks, cadaver nostril hairs, and amorous anchovies churning the ocean at the 33rd Ig Nobel ceremony
article_paragraphs_en: On September 14, 2023, the 33rd First Annual Ig Nobel Prize ceremony pushed scientific ingenuity into gothic and cyberpunk territory. Rice University engineers Te Faye Yap, Zhen Liu, Anoop Rajappan, Trevor Shimokusu, and Daniel Preston won the Mechanical Engineering Prize for inventing 'necrobotics'—re-animating dead wolf spiders to serve as mechanical gripping tools. Because spider legs lack extensor muscles and rely on internal hydraulic pressure from the cephalothorax to extend, a deceased spider naturally curls its legs into a closed fist; by gluing a hypodermic needle into the spider's body and puffing air in and out, the team created a ready-to-use biotic claw capable of lifting more than 130 percent of its own body weight over hundreds of cycles. Equally unforgettable was the Public Health Prize, awarded to Seung-min Park for inventing the 'Stanford Toilet,' a smart mountable toilet system equipped with urinalysis dipstick strips, computer-vision defecation cameras, and a biometric 'anal-print' sensor that identifies each user by the unique topography of their anus.

Across anatomy, gustation, geology, and oceanography, laureates interrogated the senses with admirable devotion. University of California, Irvine dermatology researchers Christine Pham, Bobak Hedayati, Kiana Hashemi, Ella Csuka, Tiana Mamaghani, Margit Juhasz, Jamie Wikenheiser, and Natasha Mesinkovska won the Medicine Prize for painstakingly counting the nostril hairs of twenty human cadavers, establishing that the average left nostril harbors roughly 120 hairs while the right holds 112. Japan's Homei Miyashita and Hiromi Nakamura took the Nutrition Prize for inventing electrified chopsticks and drinking straws that pass weak electric currents across the tongue to amplify saltiness without extra sodium. In the Chemistry and Geology Prize, paleontologist Jan Zalasiewicz explained why field geologists constantly lick rocks: wetting a stone's surface brings out fossil textures and mineral grains far more clearly than dry inspection. And in the Physics Prize, Bieito Fernández Castro, Marian Peña, Enrique Nogueira, Miguel Gilcoto, Esperanza Broullón, Antonio Comesaña, Damien Bouffard, Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, and Beatriz Mouriño-Carballido spent two weeks measuring coastal waters off Galicia, proving that the frenzied nocturnal spawning of millions of anchovies creates enough turbulence to mix upper ocean layers.

Studies of language, boredom, and crowd psychology completed the 2023 roster. Chris Moulin, Nicole Bell, Merita Turunen, Arina Baharin, and Akira O'Connor captured the Literature Prize by asking volunteers to write a familiar word like 'the' or 'door' dozens of times until 'jamais vu' set in and the word looked utterly alien. Communication Prize winners María José Torres-Prioris, Diana López-Barroso, Estela Càmara, Sol Fittipaldi, Lucas Sedeño, Agustín Ibáñez, Marcelo Berthier, and Adolfo García used neuroimaging to study the brains of experts who can fluently speak backward by reversing phoneme order on the fly. In the Education Prize, Katy Tam, Cyanea Poon, Victoria Hui, Wijnand van Tilburg, Christy Wong, Vivian Kwong, Gigi Yuen, and Christian Chan proved that a bored teacher's boredom directly infects students—and that merely expecting a lecture to be boring guarantees it will feel twice as dull. Finally, social psychologists Stanley Milgram, Leonard Bickman, and Lawrence Berkowitz received the Psychology Prize for their classic 1969 New York street experiment measuring how many passersby stop and crane their necks skyward when they see a crowd of strangers staring up at an empty building.

article_paragraphs: 2024年9月12日，阔别线下四年的第34届搞笑诺贝尔奖重返美国麻省理工学院礼堂，漫天纸飞机再度齐飞。已故行为主义心理学泰斗斯金纳凭二战时期的“鸽子计划”获追授和平奖——当年他训练活鸽子坐进导弹导引舱，靠不停啄击屏幕目标来引导导弹航向；福代斯·伊利与威廉·彼得森则凭1941年的经典实验获追授生物学奖，两人把一只猫放在奶牛背上并每隔两分钟捏爆一个纸袋，证实剧烈惊吓诱发的肾上腺素会瞬间锁死奶牛排乳。动物界同样在生理学奖与物理学奖中大显身手：日本学者冈部亮、芳川丰史、武部贵则等人受泥鳅启发，发现小鼠与猪等哺乳动物具备通过肛门肠道呼吸换气以缓解呼吸衰竭的绝技；哈佛大学学者廖自强则把死虹鳟鱼放进水流漩涡中，解释了死鱼如何被动利用卡门涡街的能量像活鱼一样逆流摆尾游动。

实验狂人们将耐心与脑洞推向极致。荷兰学者弗兰蒂舍克·巴托什、埃里克-扬·瓦根梅克尔斯与四十八位合作者不眠不休狂抛了三十五万零七百五十七次硬币，用铁证表明硬币落下时倾向于停留在起抛时朝上的同一面，捧走概率学奖。苔丝·希尔曼斯、安托万·德布莱、丹尼尔·邦与桑德·沃特森把水蚯蚓泡酒精灌醉后放进微柱通道迷宫，利用清醒蠕虫比醉酒蠕虫蠕动快的特性实现了“活性聚合物色谱分离”，斩获化学奖。植物学奖得主雅各布·怀特与费利佩·山下更是颠覆认知：他们发现南美变叶藤等真植物竟然能惟妙惟肖地模仿旁边人造塑料假植物叶子的形状，引发了“植物是否拥有视觉”的激烈争论。

针对人类自身的另外三项大奖给出了辛辣答案。法国与智利学者玛乔莱娜·威廉姆斯、罗曼·孔萨里等人对比南北半球人群头顶的发旋，发现南半球人逆时针发旋比例明显高于北半球，拿下解剖学奖；利文·申克、塔赫米内·法代与克里斯蒂安·比歇尔在安慰剂鼻喷雾中加入辣椒素，证实会引起火辣疼痛副作用的假药比温和无痛的假药止痛效果更好，夺得医学奖。人口学奖得主索尔·贾斯汀·纽曼则像侦探一样核查全球著名的“百岁老人长寿区”，发现那些号称盛产超百岁寿星的地方，往往只是出生死亡档案记录最混乱、文书错误频发与冒领养老金欺诈最猖獗的地区。

title_en: Missile-Guiding Pigeons, Butt-Breathing Mammals, and Drunk Worm Chromatography
subtitle_en: Returning live to MIT after four online years with 350,757 coin flips and a cat perched on a cow beside exploding paper bags
article_paragraphs_en: On the evening of September 12, 2024, the 34th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize ceremony returned to a packed auditorium at MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts—resuming the beloved in-person tradition of paper-airplane deluges after four online pandemic years. The Peace Prize was awarded posthumously to legendary behaviorist B.F. Skinner (accepted by his daughter, Julie Skinner Vargas) for his World War II 'Project Pigeon' experiments, which housed live trained pigeons inside missile nose cones to guide the weapons by pecking at target images on a screen. Equally historic was the Biology Prize, awarded posthumously to dairy scientists Fordyce Ely and William E. Petersen for their 1941 experiment placing a cat on the back of a dairy cow and exploding paper bags every two minutes to prove that fright and adrenaline completely block milk ejection. Animal physiology also amazed the crowd in the Physiology Prize—won by Ryo Okabe, Toyofumi F. Chen-Yoshikawa, Yosuke Yoneyama, Yuhei Yokoyama, Satona Tanaka, Akihiko Yoshizawa, Wendy L. Thompson, Gokul Kannan, Eiji Kobayashi, Hiroshi Date, and Takanori Takebe for discovering that mice, rats, and pigs can breathe through their anus via oxygenated liquid enemas—and the Physics Prize, won by James C. Liao for demonstrating how a dead trout can swim upstream by passively harvesting energy from Kármán vortex wakes.

Heroic persistence and laboratory ingenuity defined the physical and plant sciences in 2024. Probability Prize laureates František Bartoš, Eric-Jan Wagenmakers, Alexandra Sarafoglou, Henrik Godmann, and 44 colleagues tested mathematician Persi Diaconis's coin-precession model by flipping coins 350,757 times on video, proving that a flipped coin lands on the same side it started from roughly 50.8 percent of the time. In the Chemistry Prize, Dutch and French physicists Tess Heeremans, Antoine Deblais, Daniel Bonn, and Sander Woutersen used *Tubifex* worms as 'active polymers,' getting half of the worms drunk in ethanol and separating sober from intoxicated worms through a pillar-array chromatography channel. Meanwhile, Botany Prize winners Jacob White and Felipe Yamashita stunned biologists by showing that the South American vine *Boquila trifoliolata* can alter its leaves to mimic the shapes of neighboring artificial plastic plants, sparking fierce debate over whether plants possess a rudimentary form of vision.

Three prizes turned a sharp lens on human anatomy, medical psychology, and demographic illusions. French and Chilean researchers Marjolaine Willems, Quentin Hennocq, Sara Tunon de Lara, Nicolas Kogane, Vincent Fleury, Romy Rayssiguier, Juan José Cortés Santander, Roberto Requena, Julien Stirnemann, and Roman Hossein Khonsari earned the Anatomy Prize for comparing scalp hair whorls in Paris and Santiago, discovering that counter-clockwise hair swirls are significantly more common in the southern hemisphere than in the northern hemisphere. Medicine Prize laureates Lieven A. Schenk, Tahmine Fadai, and Christian Büchel laced inert nasal sprays with a pinch of capsaicin, demonstrating that fake medicine causing painful burning side effects relieves pain more effectively than painless placebos because patients assume discomfort signals a potent drug. Finally, Oxford demographer Saul Justin Newman won the Demography Prize for detective work exposing that the world's famed 'Blue Zones' of supercentenarians are actually regions plagued by abysmal birth-and-death recordkeeping, clerical errors, and widespread pension fraud.

article_paragraphs: 2025年9月18日，第35届搞笑诺贝尔奖将科学视野对准了餐桌美食与人间烟火。意大利与德国、西班牙学者贾科莫·巴托卢奇等八位物理学家研究经典罗马芝士黑胡椒意面的酱汁相变规律，精准测算出防止羊奶酪遇热凝结成坨的淀粉水黄金配比，斩获物理学奖。美国与以色列学者罗特姆·纳夫塔洛维奇、丹尼尔·纳夫塔洛维奇和弗兰克·格林威则在化学奖中提出奇葩减肥法：在食物里掺入不粘锅涂层塑料——聚四氟乙烯（特氟龙）粉末，既能增加食物体积撑饱肚子又绝对零卡路里。动物也难逃美食诱惑：丹尼尔·登迪与卢卡·路易塞利等人在西非多哥海滨度假村发现当地野生彩虹飞蜥偏爱挑食四重芝士披萨，摘得营养学奖；美国学者朱莉·门内拉与加里·博尚证实哺乳期母亲吃大蒜会让母乳带上蒜味，而婴儿非但不嫌弃反而吸吮更久，捧走儿科学奖。

酒精在人类与动物界引发了截然相反的喜剧效果。荷兰与英国、德国学者弗里茨·伦纳、英格·克斯伯根、马特·菲尔德与杰西卡·韦特曼让学荷兰语的德国人小酌伏特加，证实微醺状态下的“荷兰勇气”确实能显著提升外语口语发音与流利度表现，荣获和平奖；而弗朗西斯科·桑切斯、玛丽亚娜·梅尔孔、卡米·科里内与贝里·平肖在航空学奖中给埃及果蝠喂食含酒精果肉，发现醉酒蝙蝠不仅飞得跌跌撞撞，连声呐回声定位能力都严重受损。日本学者儿岛朋贵、大石风人、佐藤彩等十一人则给黑色和牛刷上白色斑马条纹，发现黑白条纹能扰乱昆虫视觉，让牛群遭受吸血蝇叮咬的次数减半，摘得生物学奖。

在日常生活细节与心理洞察上，本届得主同样令人绝倒。已故美国医学教授威廉·比恩获追授文学奖，他连续三十五年风雨无阻地坚持记录并分析自己左手拇指指甲的生长速度，写就半生微观生命史诗。波兰与澳大利亚学者马尔钦·扎延科夫斯基和吉尔·吉尼亚克发现，只要夸一句“你智商真高”，哪怕普通人也会瞬间涌起临时自恋膨胀感，拿下心理学奖；印度工程师维卡什·库马尔与萨尔塔克·米塔尔则从工程设计角度深入分析臭鞋如何破坏使用鞋架的美好体验，并重新设计出通风除臭鞋架，赢得工程设计奖。

title_en: Zebra-Striped Wagyu Cows, Zero-Calorie Teflon Diets, and the Physics of Clumping Pasta Sauce
subtitle_en: Thirty-five years of fingernail watching, pizza-snatching lizards, and tipsy bats at the 35th Ig Nobel celebration
article_paragraphs_en: On September 18, 2025, the 35th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize ceremony served up a feast of culinary physics, bizarre diets, and opportunistic appetites. Capturing the Physics Prize were Giacomo Bartolucci, Daniel Maria Busiello, Matteo Ciarchi, Alberto Corticelli, Ivan Di Terlizzi, Fabrizio Olmeda, Davide Revignas, and Vincenzo Maria Schimmenti, who mapped the phase behavior of classic Roman *Cacio e Pepe* pasta sauce, pinpointing the exact starch-to-cheese ratio required to prevent melted pecorino from clumping into unappetizing mozzarella-like globs. On the opposite end of gastronomy, Chemistry Prize winners Rotem Naftalovich, Daniel Naftalovich, and Frank Greenway proposed mixing powdered polytetrafluoroethylene—better known as non-stick Teflon plastic—into human food at up to 25 percent volume to trigger satiety with zero calories. Animals and infants displayed far better taste: Daniele Dendi, Gabriel H. Segniagbeto, Roger Meek, and Luca Luiselli won the Nutrition Prize for documenting how wild rainbow lizards at a seaside resort in Togo aggressively raid tourists' tables specifically for four-cheese pizza, while Pediatrics Prize laureates Julie Mennella and Gary Beauchamp proved that when nursing mothers eat garlic, their breast milk takes on a garlicky aroma that causes babies to latch on longer and nurse more vigorously.

Alcohol produced hilariously divergent outcomes across species in 2025. Peace Prize winners Fritz Renner, Inge Kersbergen, Matt Field, and Jessica Werthmann gave German native speakers who had recently learned Dutch a modest dose of vodka-spiked bitter lemon, proving that 'Dutch courage' genuinely improves observers' ratings of foreign-language pronunciation and fluency. Conversely, Aviation Prize laureates Francisco Sánchez, Mariana Melcón, Carmi Korine, and Berry Pinshow fed ethanol-laden fruit juice to Egyptian fruit bats and found that tipsy bats fly sluggishly through obstacle courses and slur their echolocation calls. Meanwhile, in Japanese pastures, Tomoki Kojima, Kazato Oishi, Yasushi Matsubara, Yuki Uchiyama, Yoshihiko Fukushima, Naoto Aoki, Say Sato, Tatsuaki Masuda, Junichi Ueda, Hiroyuki Hirooka, and Katsutoshi Kino won the Biology Prize for painting black Wagyu cows with white zebra stripes, cutting biting-fly attacks by more than half.

Rounding out the 35th anniversary were studies of lifelong patience, fragile egos, and malodorous footwear. The Literature Prize was awarded posthumously to Dr. William B. Bean (accepted by his son, Bennett Bean), who scored a mark into his left thumbnail at age 32 and meticulously recorded its growth rate for 35 consecutive years across six medical papers, chronicling how his nail slowed as he aged. In the Psychology Prize, Marcin Zajenkowski and Gilles Gignac demonstrated that simply telling people they scored high on an IQ test immediately inflates a temporary state of narcissistic uniqueness, even in non-narcissists. Finally, Indian engineers Vikash Kumar and Sarthak Mittal earned the Engineering Design Prize for analyzing how foul-smelling sweaty shoes ruin the user experience of household shoe racks and engineering a ventilated, heated rack to banish the stench.

article_paragraphs: 2026年9月3日，第36届搞笑诺贝尔奖首次走出美国本土，移师瑞士苏黎世热闹开奖。东道主瑞士学者弗朗茨·本德、马塞尔·范德海登与阿特兰特·比耶里、皮娅·维维亚尼主场斩获土壤科学奖：他们在超过二十五个国家的泥土里埋下一千条一模一样的纯棉白内裤，两个月后挖出来，用内裤被土壤微生物和蚯蚓啃成破洞装的程度来评估土壤生态健康。同样在自然界玩命探索的还有生物学奖得主、巴西学者若昂·米格尔·阿尔维斯-努涅斯等六人——他穿上特制防毒靴，在不同气温与时段反复轻轻踩踏各种毒蛇的头、腹、尾部数万次，以弄清究竟什么情况会诱发毒蛇咬人。

微观工程与流体物理领域的成果令人叹为观止。加拿大麦吉尔大学的贾斯汀·普马、杨震、张子馨、李剑宇与曹长虹等十二位学者把死蚊子吸血的纤细口器拆下来当作超高分辨率三维打印喷嘴，开创“死灵打印”技术，摘得技术奖。桑查里·班纳吉、伦纳德·沙瓦斯与苏布拉马尼扬·拉马斯瓦米等人解析了胎生太平洋折翅蠊哺育后代的蛋白晶体，发现这种“蟑螂奶”所含能量竟然高达普通牛奶蛋白的三倍，夺得化学奖。兰迪·赫德、潘钊、塔德·特拉斯科特与卡维尚·图赖拉贾则通过理论微分方程与流体实验，设计出尿流撞击角恒小于临界角、彻底告别尿滴乱溅的“零飞溅小便池”，捧走物理学奖。

关于人类与动物社交天性的奖项同样妙趣横生。英国牛津大学的玛蒂尔达·布林德尔、凯瑟琳·塔尔博特与斯图尔特·韦斯特为“接吻”拟定了“非敌对同种口对口接触且无食物传递”的精确科学定义，证实蚂蚁、鸟类和北极熊也会接吻，荣膺生物力学奖；日本已故学者海野德二凭《擤鼻涕的空气动力学研究》获追授医学奖。伊洛娜·克罗伊与阿格涅什卡·索罗科夫斯卡等人证实婴儿闻起来对父母美妙无比、但青少年闻起来却令父母嫌弃，拿下嗅觉奖；保罗·皮夫与达切尔·克尔特纳等人收集证据表明上流阶层富人更容易顺手牵羊抢走留给儿童的糖果并做出不道德行为，摘得经济学奖；而杰米·阿罗娜·克雷姆斯与丹尼尔·斯尼策等人则证实，人们十分看重那些对我们讨厌的人表现出刻薄凶狠态度的朋友，赢得和平奖。

title_en: 1,000 Buried Underpants, Mosquito-Snout 3D Printing, and Stepping on Venomous Snakes 40,000 Times
subtitle_en: Making history in Zurich, Switzerland with high-energy cockroach milk crystals, splash-free urinals, and vicious friends
article_paragraphs_en: On September 3, 2026, the 36th First Annual Ig Nobel Prize ceremony made history by staging its live gala outside the United States for the first time, convening in Zurich, Switzerland. Fittingly, Swiss soil scientists Franz Bender, Marcel van der Heijden, Atlant Bieri, and Pia Viviani triumphed on home turf with the Soil Science Prize: enlisting citizen scientists across more than 25 countries, they buried 1,000 identical pairs of white cotton underpants and dug them up two months later, quantifying soil ecosystem health by how thoroughly microbes and earthworms had munched the fabric into lace. Equally daring fieldwork earned the Biology Prize for Brazilian herpetologists João Miguel Alves-Nunes, Adriano Fellone, Selma Maria Almeida-Santos, Carlos Roberto de Medeiros, Ivan Sazima, and Otavio Augusto Vuolo Marques. Wearing padded bite-proof boots, Alves-Nunes gently stepped on the heads, midbodies, and tails of venomous jararaca pit vipers over 40,000 times at various temperatures and times of day, proving that smaller, female snakes stepped on near the head in warm weather are far more likely to strike.

Micro-engineering, biochemistry, and bathroom fluid mechanics reached dazzling heights in 2026. Technology Prize laureates Justin Puma, Zhen Yang, Evan Johnston, Zixin Zhang, Xiaoyi Lan, Lingzhi Zhang, Hongyu Hou, Zixin He, Ali Afify, Megan Creighton, Jianyu Li, and Changhong Cao pioneered '3D Necroprinting,' harvesting the 20-micron proboscises of dead female mosquitoes to serve as ultra-high-resolution, biodegradable 3D-printing nozzles. In the Chemistry Prize, Sanchari Banerjee, Nathan Coussens, François-Xavier Gallat, Nitish Sathyanarayanan, Jandhyam Srikanth, Koichiro Yagi, James Gray, Stephen Tobe, Barbara Stay, Leonard Chavas, and Subramanian Ramaswamy solved the atomic structure of protein crystals secreted by the viviparous cockroach *Diploptera punctata* to nourish its embryos, revealing that 'cockroach milk' packs three times the energy density of dairy cow milk. Meanwhile, physicists Randy Hurd, Zhao Pan, Tadd Truscott, and Kaveeshan Thurairajah won the Physics Prize for using differential equations and synthetic urine jets to design a nautilus-inspired 'splash-free urinal' whose curved walls keep the stream impact angle below the critical 30-degree splatter threshold.

Studies of kissing, nose-blowing, body odor, and social morality completed the Zurich celebration. Oxford biologists Matilda Brindle, Catherine Talbot, and Stuart West won the Biomechanics Prize for crafting a rigorously unromantic definition of kissing—'non-agonistic interactions involving directed, intraspecific, oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer'— across ants, birds, polar bears, and humans. The Medicine Prize was awarded posthumously to Japan's Tokuji Unno for his 1977 aerodynamic study of human nose-blowing, while Olfaction Prize winners Ilona Croy, Tomasz Frackowiak, Thomas Hummel, and Agnieszka Sorokowska proved that while babies smell wonderful to their parents, teenagers decidedly do not. Finally, social scientists exposed our darker instincts: Paul Piff, Daniel Stancato, Stéphane Côté, Rodolfo Mendoza-Denton, and Dacher Keltner won the Economics Prize for showing that upper-class individuals are more likely to cut off pedestrians in luxury cars and snatch candy explicitly reserved for children, while Peace Prize laureates Jaimie Arona Krems, Rebecka Hahnel-Peeters, Laureon Merrie, Keelah Williams, and Daniel Sznycer documented that humans secretly value friends who are vicious toward our enemies.
